title: In-between animals: mammals that lay eggs, fish that breathe air, and what the five groups tell us about evolution

summary.text: A platypus has fur and feeds her babies milk, yet she lays eggs. A murrel is a fish, yet she comes up to breathe air. In this lesson you will test how much air cold and warm water hold, put animal features in order of arrival, and find old leftover parts in your body.
summary.art: Three small scenes side by side: a platypus curled round two small eggs in a burrow, a long dark fish with her mouth at the surface of a muddy tank making a ring on the water, and a crow on a window grill with the faint outline of a small feathered dinosaur behind her.

intro.hook: Which came first in the history of animals: lungs or legs? And which came first: milk, or babies born without an egg? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Many people guess that lungs and legs arrived together, when animals first moved onto land. Many also guess that birth came before milk. In the first activity, the Feature Ladder, you tick the features of seven animals and read the order from your own table. Two animals settle the question: a fish with lungs and a mammal who lays eggs. Then you test why a fish would ever need to breathe air.
intro.art: A child at a table with a sheet of paper ruled into a table, with small drawings of a carp, a lungfish, a frog, a crocodile, a pigeon, a platypus and a cow down the side.

outcomes: I can explain that the five groups of vertebrates are branches of one family tree, and that their features arrived one at a time.
I can explain why some fish breathe air, using what I found about the air dissolved in cold and warm water.
I can describe how fins became limbs, and say what the fossils Tiktaalik and Acanthostega showed.
I can explain how the platypus and the echidnas show that milk is older than birth without an egg.
I can say why birds are dinosaurs, and why a crocodile is a closer relative of a crow than of a lizard.
I can tell a likeness that comes from a shared ancestor from a likeness that arose separately, and give live birth as an example.
I can find leftover features in my own body, and say how fossils, bodies and DNA are used as evidence for the family tree.
I can run a fair test, record the results in a table, and say what I think, what I saw and why.

terms.meaning: A vertebrate is an animal with a backbone. Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are all vertebrates.
terms.example: A sardine, a frog, a house gecko, a crow and you are all vertebrates.
terms.art: Five small animals in a row, a sardine, a frog, a gecko, a crow and a girl, each with the backbone drawn in as a white line.

terms.meaning: Evolution is the slow change of living beings over many generations. Young are a little different from their parents, and over millions of years the small differences add up.
terms.example: Over about ten million years, the fins of some fish became limbs with fingers.
terms.art: A row of five animals from a fish with fleshy fins to a four-legged animal, each a little different from the one before.

terms.meaning: An ancestor is a relative who lived before you and from whom you descend. Your grandmother is an ancestor. So is an animal who lived millions of years ago, if her line of young leads to you.
terms.example: A crow and a crocodile share an ancestor who lived about 240 to 250 million years ago.
terms.art: A family line drawn as dots going back in time, with one dot far back circled and two lines leading from it to a crow and a crocodile.

terms.meaning: The family tree of life is a drawing that shows how living beings are related. Each fork is an ancestor whose young went two different ways.
terms.example: On the family tree, the branch with frogs splits off before the branch with lizards and the branch with mammals.
terms.art: A simple branching tree drawn sideways with small animals at the tips: a carp, a lungfish, a frog, a lizard, a crow and a cow.

terms.meaning: A branch of the family tree is one ancestor together with all of her descendants. Scientists also call a branch a clade.
terms.example: All mammals form one branch. All birds form one branch, and that branch sits inside the dinosaur branch.
terms.art: A tree with one fork and everything growing from it shaded in one colour, to show a whole branch.

terms.meaning: A feature is a part of a body, or a way a body works, that can be compared between animals. Scientists also call a feature a trait.
terms.example: Lungs, feathers, fur, milk and a shelled egg are all features.
terms.art: Five small labelled drawings: a pair of lungs, a feather, a tuft of fur, a drop of milk and an egg.

terms.meaning: Dissolved oxygen is oxygen gas that is mixed into water, too finely to see. Fish take this oxygen out of the water with their gills.
terms.example: A litre of cool river water holds about 9 milligrams of dissolved oxygen. A litre of air holds about 30 times as much.
terms.art: A tumbler of clear water with a zoom-in circle showing a few small oxygen particles spread among many water particles.

terms.meaning: An air-breathing fish is a fish who can take oxygen from air as well as from water. She swims up and gulps air at the surface.
terms.example: The murrel and the climbing perch of Indian ponds are air-breathing fish.
terms.art: A murrel at the surface of a pond with her mouth just out of the water and a ring spreading round her.

terms.meaning: A lobe-finned fish has thick, fleshy fins with bones and muscles inside. Lungfish and coelacanths are the lobe-finned fish alive today.
terms.example: The bones inside a lungfish's fin match the bones of your upper arm.
terms.art: A fleshy fin drawn in cross-section with one bone at the base and smaller bones beyond, beside a thin fan-shaped fin of a carp.

terms.meaning: A tetrapod is a vertebrate with four limbs, or one whose ancestors had four limbs. Amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are tetrapods.
terms.example: A snake is a tetrapod, because her ancestors were lizards with four legs.
terms.art: A frog, a gecko, a crow, a cow and a snake in a row, with the four limbs marked on each and faint dotted legs on the snake.

terms.meaning: A fossil is what is left of a living being from long ago, kept in rock. Bones, shells, eggs and footprints can all become fossils.
terms.example: Fossil dinosaur eggs lie in the rocks near Balasinor in Gujarat.
terms.art: A slab of rock with the flat outline of a fish skeleton pressed into it.

terms.meaning: A transitional fossil is a fossil with some features of an older group and some of a newer group. It shows what the animals in between looked like.
terms.example: Tiktaalik had scales and gills like a fish, and a neck and wrists like a four-limbed animal.
terms.art: A flat-headed fish-like animal propped on two sturdy front fins at the edge of a shallow stream.

terms.meaning: The amnion is a thin bag of water that surrounds a growing baby reptile, bird or mammal. It lets the baby grow away from ponds and streams, inside a shelled egg or inside the mother.
terms.example: A chick inside an egg and a calf inside a cow both float in an amnion.
terms.art: An egg cut open to show a small chick floating in a clear bag of water, beside a calf curled up inside the same kind of bag.

terms.meaning: A monotreme is a mammal who lays eggs. There are five kinds alive: the platypus and four kinds of echidna.
terms.example: A platypus mother lays about two soft-shelled eggs and then feeds the hatched babies on milk.
terms.art: A platypus and a spiny echidna side by side, each with a small round egg beside them.

terms.meaning: The placenta is a part that grows inside a pregnant mammal mother. It passes food and oxygen from her blood to the baby until birth.
terms.example: You were fed through a placenta before you were born. Your navel marks where the cord from the placenta joined you.
terms.art: A baby curled inside the mother's body, joined by a cord to a flat disc on the wall around the baby.

terms.meaning: Convergent evolution happens when the same feature arises separately in animals who are not close relatives. The likeness comes from a similar way of living, and not from a shared ancestor.
terms.example: Bats and birds both have wings, but their shared ancestor had none. Wings arose twice.
terms.art: A bat and a bird flying side by side, with the different bones inside each wing drawn in.

terms.meaning: A vestigial part is a small leftover of a part that was bigger and did more in an animal's ancestors.
terms.example: Your tailbone is a vestigial part. It is what is left of a tail.
terms.art: A human skeleton seen from the side with the small tailbone at the bottom of the backbone circled.

terms.meaning: DNA is the long molecule in every cell that carries the instructions for building a body. Parents pass copies of their DNA to their young.
terms.example: The more alike the DNA of two animals is, the more recently they shared an ancestor.
terms.art: A twisted ladder shape with four kinds of rung, and two short strips of letters below with one letter different.

explanations.concept: The five groups are branches of one family tree
explanations.definition: All vertebrates descend from one group of small, fish-like animals who lived about 500 million years ago. The five groups we name today are branches that split off from that one family at different times.
explanations.description: In Class 3 you learnt how the five groups breathe, keep warm and have young. In Class 4 you learnt how they sense the world. Now ask a different question. Why are there groups at all? The answer is that animals are related, as cousins are. Long ago one population of animals split into two, and each half went on changing in its own way. This happened again and again. Animals whose shared ancestor lived recently are still much alike, so we put them in one group. Animals whose shared ancestor lived very long ago have had more time to grow different. So a group is a set of close relatives. This also explains the animals who do not fit neatly. Between any two groups there were once animals in between. Most of them died out, and that is why the groups look so separate today. When one of the in-between animals is still alive, like the platypus, or turns up as a fossil, the gap between two groups closes a little.
examples: A crow and a sparrow share an ancestor who lived some tens of millions of years ago, so they are much alike.
A crow and a carp share an ancestor who lived more than 400 million years ago, so they are very different.
The platypus has fur and milk like other mammals and lays eggs like a reptile or a bird. Her branch split from ours very early.
explanations.art: A tree drawn sideways with a time line under it, the five groups at the branch tips, and faint dotted twigs that end early to show relatives who died out.

explanations.concept: The features of a group arrived one at a time
explanations.definition: No group got all of its features at once. Each feature first appeared in one ancestor, and only the animals descended from that ancestor carry it.
explanations.description: In the Feature Ladder you ticked the features of seven animals. The ticks made steps. Every animal had a backbone. All but the carp had lungs. Five had four limbs. Four grew inside an amnion. Two had fur and milk. Only the cow was born alive after being fed through a placenta. The steps show the order in which the features arrived. The backbone came first. Lungs came before limbs, because the lungfish has lungs and no limbs. The amnion came after limbs. Milk came before birth without an egg, because the platypus has milk and still lays eggs. So the list we learn for each group, such as 'a mammal has fur, gives milk and is born alive', was never one set. It was built up one feature at a time over millions of years. Be careful with the ladder in one way. It shows the order of branching. It does not show that the animals on the higher steps are better. Every animal on the ladder is alive today, and every one of them has been evolving for exactly the same length of time.
examples: Backbone: about 500 million years old. Fingers and toes: about 365 million years old. Milk: more than 200 million years old.
A frog has lungs and four limbs but no amnion. Her eggs must stay wet, so most frogs lay them in water.
Feathers are a feature of a side branch. In the Feature Ladder only the pigeon had them.
explanations.art: A staircase of six steps labelled backbone, lungs, four limbs, amnion, fur and milk, born alive, with one of the seven animals standing on each step and the pigeon beside the crocodile.

explanations.definition: Water holds very little oxygen, and warm, still water holds least. Fish who live in warm, still water often have a second way to get oxygen: they swim up and gulp air.
explanations.description: A fish breathes with gills. Gills are thin, feathery sheets full of blood, and they take dissolved oxygen out of the water that flows over them. There is not much to take. A litre of water at 20 °C holds about 9 milligrams of oxygen. A litre of air holds about 30 times as much. In the Air in Water test you saw what warmth does. The cold water gave up bubbles of air as it warmed, because warm water cannot hold as much dissolved air as cold water. Now think of a village tank or a paddy field in May. The water is shallow, still and warm. Rotting leaves use up oxygen too, and so do the water plants at night. By dawn there may be almost no oxygen left, and fish with gills alone crowd at the surface and gasp. Some fish have another way. The murrel has a chamber above her gills, lined with thin skin full of blood. She swims up, gulps a mouthful of air into the chamber, and takes the oxygen from it. The climbing perch has folded plates of thin bone in the same place. The mudskipper of our mangroves takes in oxygen through her wet skin and through the lining of her mouth and throat. The murrel and the climbing perch depend on air so much that they must reach the surface to live. Kept under water with no way up, they can drown.
examples: Murrels and climbing perches are sold alive in wet baskets in markets in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, West Bengal and Assam, because they can breathe air for hours.
A fighting fish in a small bowl swims up to gulp air every few minutes. She is a relative of the climbing perch.
Mudskippers hop over the wet mud at Point Calimere in Tamil Nadu and at Coringa in Andhra Pradesh.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a murrel's head showing the gills and, above them, an air chamber with a bubble of air inside, and an arrow from her mouth at the water surface.

explanations.definition: Lungs first appeared in fish, more than 400 million years ago, long before any animal had legs. Land animals did not invent lungs. They inherited them.
explanations.description: A lung is a bag that opens off the throat and has thin walls full of blood. A fish who gulps air into such a bag gets oxygen from the air. Lungfish have lungs that work as ours do. Six kinds of lungfish are alive today, in Africa, South America and Australia. The South American lungfish must breathe air to live. Lungfish in Africa and South America can also lie in the mud right through the dry season and breathe air until the rain returns. Another fish with lungs is the bichir of Africa. The bichir's branch split off very early from the branch of most other fish. Because both lungfish and bichirs have lungs, scientists conclude that the shared ancestor of all bony fish had lungs too. So where are the lungs of a carp or a sardine? They are still there, changed into something else. Most fish today have a swim bladder, a bag of gas that keeps them from sinking. The swim bladder grows from the same place as a lung. Charles Darwin guessed that lungs came from swim bladders. The evidence now points the other way. The swim bladder is a changed lung.
examples: Your lungs and a lungfish's lungs come from the same ancestor's lungs.
The swim bladder of a rohu is the silver balloon you may have seen when a fish is cleaned at the market.
When Tiktaalik's relatives moved into shallow water about 375 million years ago, they already had lungs.
explanations.art: Three fish in a row cut open to show a lung in a bichir, a lung in a lungfish, and a silver swim bladder in a carp, with an arrow from 'lung' to 'swim bladder'.

explanations.concept: From fin to limb: Tiktaalik and Acanthostega
explanations.definition: Limbs with fingers and toes evolved from the fleshy fins of lobe-finned fish, between about 375 and 365 million years ago. Fossils show the stages in between.
explanations.description: Feel your arm. There is one bone in the upper arm, two bones in the lower arm, many small bones in the wrist, and then fingers. A frog's front leg, a crow's wing and a whale's flipper all have this same pattern. A lobe-finned fish has the beginning of the pattern inside each fleshy fin: one bone, then two. In 2004, Edward Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins found a fossil in rocks about 375 million years old on Ellesmere Island, in the far north of Canada. They named her Tiktaalik. She had scales and gills like a fish. She also had a flat head, a neck that let her turn her head, strong ribs, and fins with a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist. She could prop herself up in shallow water. She had no fingers yet. Acanthostega lived about ten million years later, in what is now Greenland. She had four limbs with fingers, eight on each hand. Yet she still had gills, and her limbs and ribs were too weak to hold her up on land. So the first limbs with fingers were used in water. Walking on land came later.
examples: One bone, two bones, many small bones, fingers: the same pattern is inside your arm, a bat's wing and a dolphin's flipper.
Tiktaalik had a neck. A fish has none, so she must turn her whole body to look sideways.
Five fingers is not the oldest number. Acanthostega had eight.
explanations.art: Three limbs in a row with the bones drawn in and matching bones in matching colours: the fleshy fin of a lobe-finned fish, the fin of Tiktaalik with a wrist, and the eight-fingered limb of Acanthostega.

explanations.concept: Why did animals with limbs first leave the water?
explanations.description: Limbs and lungs were both there before any vertebrate lived on land. So something else must explain why some of these animals began to spend time out of the water. Nobody watched it happen, and the fossils do not say why. Scientists have several ideas, and more than one may be true.
examples: Insects, millipedes and plants were living on land long before the first vertebrate walked there.
Fossils of the early limbed animals are found in rocks from wet, wooded river plains, not from deserts.
Mudskippers today leave the water to feed on the mud and to escape fish who hunt them.

perspectives.explanation: The American scientist Alfred Romer argued in the 1900s that ponds dried up, and fish who could crawl to the next pond survived. Few scientists accept this now. The first limbs were too weak for crawling, and the fossils come from wet places.

perspectives.who: Food and safety at the edge
perspectives.explanation: The shallow edges of rivers were full of small animals to eat and had no large fish to fear. An animal who could push into the shallows and onto the bank found food that no one else was using. Many scientists favour this idea.

Warm, shallow water holds little oxygen. A flat head and a neck let an animal lift the nose into the air without swimming up. On this idea the body changed for breathing first, and walking was a later use for it.

explanations.art: A wooded river bank 365 million years ago with a limbed fish-like animal resting half in the water, small millipedes on the mud and tall fern-like plants behind.

explanations.definition: The platypus and the four kinds of echidna are mammals who lay eggs. They are called monotremes, and they live in Australia and New Guinea.
explanations.description: A platypus has fur. She makes milk. Her body makes its own heat, and stays at about 32 °C, a little cooler than ours. All of this makes her a mammal. Yet she lays about two small eggs, each about 17 millimetres long, with soft, leathery shells. She curls round them in a burrow for about ten days until they hatch. An echidna mother lays one egg and carries it in a pouch on her belly. The babies hatch tiny and unfinished, and then they drink milk for months. A monotreme mother has no teats. Her milk comes out through small openings in a patch of skin, and the babies take it from her fur. How can one animal have milk and eggs? The answer is in the order of the features. The early ancestors of all mammals laid eggs. Milk began in those egg-laying ancestors. The branch that leads to the platypus split off at that point, between about 160 and 220 million years ago. On the other branch, much later, the eggs came to be kept inside the mother, and the placenta evolved. So the platypus is not a mixture of a duck and a beaver. She is a mammal whose branch kept an old way of having young.
examples: A platypus baby drinks milk for about four months.
The four echidnas are the short-beaked echidna of Australia and New Guinea and three long-beaked echidnas of New Guinea.
Kangaroos and other pouched mammals are on our side of the split. Their babies are born alive, very small, and finish growing in the pouch.
explanations.art: A platypus mother curled in a burrow with two small round eggs held between her belly and her tail, and a small drawing of a hatched baby taking milk from the fur on her belly.

explanations.concept: Milk is older than birth without an egg, and your DNA shows it
explanations.definition: Milk evolved while the ancestors of mammals still laid eggs. As milk took over the feeding of the young, egg yolk was needed less and less, and in most mammals the instructions for making yolk broke down.
explanations.description: A hen's egg must hold all the food a chick needs until hatching. That food is the yolk. The body makes yolk by following instructions in the DNA, called yolk genes. In 2008, David Brawand, Walter Wahli and Henrik Kaessmann looked for these genes in mammals. Hens have three working yolk genes. The platypus has one that still works, and her small eggs do hold some yolk. Humans and dogs have none that work. But the broken pieces of the old yolk genes are still there in our DNA, in the place where a hen has hers. The same study found that the genes for the main proteins of milk were already present in the shared ancestor of all mammals. So the order was this. First, egg-laying ancestors began to make milk. Then, over a very long time, yolk was needed less, and the yolk genes stopped working one by one. You carry in every cell the worn-out instructions for making an egg yolk. One thing is still unknown. Nobody is sure what the very first milk was for. One idea is that it kept the soft-shelled eggs moist and free of germs, and that the hatched young began to lick it later.
examples: A platypus egg is small and has little yolk, because milk does most of the feeding after hatching.
A hen's egg is large for her body, because the yolk must do all the feeding.
Broken yolk genes in humans sit beside the same neighbouring genes as the working yolk genes of a hen.
explanations.art: Three strips of DNA one above the other, labelled hen, platypus and human: three bright blocks on the hen's, one bright and two faded on the platypus's, and three faded, cracked blocks on the human's.

explanations.definition: An animal who has some old features is not an old or unfinished animal. Every living animal has been evolving for the same length of time, and each has new features of her own.
explanations.description: People often call the platypus, the lungfish or the coelacanth a 'living fossil', as if they had stopped changing. This is a mistake. The platypus kept egg-laying, but her branch also evolved things that no ancestor had. When she dives, she shuts her eyes, ears and nose. She finds prawns and insect young in the mud with her bill, which holds about 40,000 sensors for the tiny electric signals that moving muscles give off. A male platypus has a spur on each back ankle that injects venom. In the same way, the murrel's air chamber is a new feature of her branch, and not a half-made lung. So there are no higher and lower animals on the family tree. There are only branches, and each branch has kept some old features and gained some new ones. This is true of us as well. Humans kept five fingers, which is an old feature. Horses changed theirs to one.
examples: The coelacanth was known only from fossils and thought to have died out 65 million years ago. In 1938 Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, who ran a small museum in East London, South Africa, spotted one in a fishing boat's catch.
The murrel's air chamber is found in no early fish. Her branch evolved it.
A snake lost her legs. Losing a feature is evolution too.
explanations.art: A platypus swimming under water with eyes closed, her bill sweeping over the mud, and faint ripple lines coming from a small prawn hidden under a stone.

explanations.concept: Birds are dinosaurs, so what is a reptile?
explanations.description: Fossils and DNA agree that birds are a branch of the dinosaurs. They also agree that crocodiles are the closest living relatives of birds. The line that leads to crocodiles and the line that leads to dinosaurs and birds split about 240 to 250 million years ago. Lizards and snakes split off earlier still. So a mugger crocodile is a closer relative of a crow than of a monitor lizard, even though she looks far more like the lizard. There are signs of this in how they live. A crocodile mother builds a nest, guards it, and answers her young when they call from inside the eggs, much as a bird does. This raises a question about names. The old group 'reptiles' holds lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles, and leaves birds out. But birds grew out of that same branch. Scientists agree on the family tree. They do not all agree on how to use the old word.
examples: A crow and a mugger crocodile share an ancestor who is not an ancestor of any lizard.
Crocodiles and birds both build nests and guard their eggs.
Scaly legs and feet on a hen are the same kind of scales that a crocodile has.

perspectives.explanation: Most scientists who draw family trees say a group should be an ancestor and all of her descendants. On this view, either birds are reptiles, or 'reptile' is not the name of a real branch. Many now say that birds are reptiles.

Others say 'reptile' is still a useful word for scaly animals who take their warmth from outside and lay shelled eggs on land. On this view a group can describe a way of living, as long as we remember that it is not a whole branch.

explanations.art: A small family tree with three tips, a monitor lizard, a mugger crocodile and a crow, where the crocodile and the crow share a fork that the lizard is not on.

explanations.concept: The same feature can arise many times
explanations.definition: When the same feature arises separately in animals who are not close relatives, it is called convergent evolution. Such a feature tells us about a way of living, and not about who is related to whom.
explanations.description: Some features are good clues to the family tree, because they arose only once. Milk arose once. Feathers arose once. Other features have arisen again and again. Giving birth to live young is the best example. The scientist Daniel Blackburn counted how many separate times it arose among vertebrates. He found more than 150 times, and at least 115 of these were in lizards and snakes. The Russell's viper, the saw-scaled viper and the common sand boa of India all bear live young, while the cobra and the rat snake lay eggs. Some sharks, the guppy and some frogs bear live young too. Among mammals it arose only once. So 'born alive' sounds like a mammal feature, but it is a poor clue to family. A warm body that makes its own heat arose separately in birds and in mammals. Wings arose separately in birds, in bats and in the extinct flying reptiles called pterosaurs. A long body with no legs arose in snakes, in some lizards and in the legless amphibians called caecilians. Why does the same answer keep turning up? Because bodies meet the same problems. A baby who grows inside the mother is safe from egg thieves and from cold. Any branch in which mothers began to keep their eggs inside for longer could go that way.
examples: A Russell's viper may give birth to 20 to 40 live young at a time.

In 2012 a new family of caecilians was named from the soil of Northeast India, after about 250 digs over five years by Rachunliu Kamei, S. D. Biju and their team. The mothers stay wrapped round their eggs for two to three months.
A dolphin and a shark have the same smooth shape for fast swimming, but one is a mammal and the other a fish.
explanations.art: Four mothers with newborn live young beside them: a viper, a guppy, a shark and a cow, with a small label 'arose separately' under each.

explanations.definition: Bodies keep leftovers of parts that did more in their ancestors. These leftovers are called vestigial parts, and they are evidence of where an animal came from.
explanations.description: Evolution does not start again from nothing. It changes what is already there, and often a small leftover stays. You carry several. At the bottom of your backbone is the tailbone, made of three to five small bones joined together. It is what is left of a tail. Before you were born, when you were about five to eight weeks old inside your mother, you had a small tail, and then your body took it back in. When you are cold, a tiny muscle at the root of each hair pulls the hair upright, and you get goosebumps. On a furry mammal this fluffs the coat and holds in more warm air. On your thin body hair it does very little. Whales have leftovers too. A whale has no back legs, but deep inside her body lie small hip bones. They fit with a find from India. In rocks about 48 million years old in Kashmir, the geologist A. Ranga Rao collected the bones of a small hoofed animal, about the size of a fox, now called Indohyus. In 2007, Hans Thewissen and his team showed that she had a thick ear bone found only in whales, and heavy bones for wading. She was a close relative of the first whales. The closest living relatives of whales today are hippos.
examples: Some people can wiggle their ears a little. The small muscles round the ear turn the ears of a dog or a cow towards a sound.
A long tendon in the wrist, called the palmaris longus, is missing in roughly one person in seven worldwide. The share differs a great deal from one part of the world to another.
Some pythons have two tiny claws near the tail, the leftovers of back legs.
explanations.art: A whale drawn from the side with the small hip bones shown inside her body, and below her a small four-legged hoofed animal wading in a river.

explanations.concept: How scientists check the family tree with DNA
explanations.definition: DNA is copied from parent to young with rare small mistakes. The longer two animals have been on separate branches, the more differences have built up between their DNA. Counting the differences shows who is related to whom.
explanations.description: For two hundred years scientists built the family tree from bones and bodies alone. Then a second kind of evidence arrived. Every cell carries DNA, a long molecule made of four kinds of unit that we write as the letters A, T, G and C. When DNA is copied for the next generation, a letter is now and then copied wrongly, and the change is passed on. So two branches that have been apart for a long time differ by many letters. The same is true of proteins, the molecules that DNA gives the instructions for. In 1965 the American scientist Margaret Dayhoff collected every protein sequence then known, 65 of them, into one book. In 1966 she and Richard Eck used a computer to build family trees from such sequences. It was the first time anyone had done this. The trees built from molecules matched the trees built from bones in almost every place. Where they did not match, scientists looked again. That is how we learnt that whales are close relatives of hippos, and that crocodiles are close relatives of birds. Two separate kinds of evidence giving the same tree is strong evidence that the tree is real.
examples: Human DNA and chimpanzee DNA differ in far fewer places than human DNA and hen DNA.
The platypus's DNA was read in full in 2008. It showed both the yolk gene of an egg-layer and the milk genes of a mammal.
DNA can also tell which fish a piece of fish in a market came from.
explanations.art: Three short strips of letters one above the other, labelled human, cow and hen, with the letters that differ from the human strip circled: few on the cow's, more on the hen's.

explanations.concept: Moving continents carried the branches apart
explanations.definition: The continents move very slowly over millions of years. When a piece of land splits, the animals on each piece go on evolving separately. So where an old branch lives today can show how the land once fitted together.
explanations.description: The family tree of vertebrates grew on a moving Earth. About 150 million years ago India was joined to Africa, Madagascar, Australia and Antarctica in one great southern land. India broke away, drifted north as an island for tens of millions of years, and met Asia about 50 million years ago. Some animals rode on India the whole way. The purple frog of the Western Ghats lives underground and comes up for a few days in the monsoon. S. D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt described her in 2003. Her closest living relatives live on the Seychelles islands, far out in the Indian Ocean. The Seychelles were once joined to India. The frogs did not cross the sea. The land split under their ancestors. The egg-laying mammals tell a similar story. They survive only in Australia and New Guinea, which have been cut off from the other continents for a very long time.
examples: The purple frog of Kerala and Tamil Nadu has her nearest relatives on islands about 3,000 kilometres away.
Fossil dinosaur eggs in Gujarat were laid when India was still an island on its way north.
In rocks about 68 million years old at Dholi Dungri in Gujarat, a fossil snake 3.5 metres long was found coiled round a dinosaur egg, beside a hatchling.
explanations.art: A map of the Indian Ocean long ago with India drawn as an island moving north, a small frog on India and a small frog on a fragment labelled Seychelles.

agreed.text: All vertebrates share one ancestor, and the five groups are branches of one family tree.
agreed.evidence: Family trees built from bones and trees built from DNA were made separately, and they match in almost every place. Fossils of the right age fill the gaps between the groups.

agreed.text: Four-limbed animals evolved from lobe-finned fish.
agreed.evidence: The bones inside a lungfish's fin match the bones of our limbs. Fossils such as Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, and Acanthostega, about 365 million years old, have mixes of fish and four-limbed features.

agreed.text: Lungs evolved in fish, before limbs.
agreed.evidence: Lungfish and bichirs, on two very different branches of bony fish, both have lungs. Tiktaalik and Acanthostega had gills and signs of air breathing together.

agreed.text: Monotremes are mammals, and milk evolved before birth without an egg.
agreed.evidence: The platypus and the echidnas have fur and milk and lay eggs. The platypus's DNA, read in 2008, has milk genes shared with all mammals and one working yolk gene. Other mammals have only broken yolk genes.

agreed.text: Birds are dinosaurs, and crocodiles are the closest living relatives of birds.
agreed.evidence: Fossil dinosaurs with feathers and wishbones have been found since 1996, and the DNA of crocodiles is closer to that of birds than to that of lizards.

agreed.text: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water.
agreed.evidence: It has been measured many times. A litre of fresh water holds about 11.3 milligrams of oxygen at 10 °C, about 9.1 at 20 °C and about 7.6 at 30 °C.

challenging.claim: Fish grew legs so that they could walk on land.
challenging.who: A common way of telling the story, and older textbooks
challenging.for: Legs are what land animals walk on, so it seems they must have evolved for walking.
challenging.against: Acanthostega had four limbs with fingers, but she had gills, and her limbs and ribs were too weak to hold her up on land. The first limbs were used in water. Also, no animal grows a part because she will need it later. A part spreads only if it helps at the time.
challenging.context: This card is about why limbs with fingers first evolved.

challenging.claim: The platypus is a primitive animal, left over from the past.
challenging.who: Many books and films, which call her a 'living fossil'
challenging.for: She lays eggs, as the early ancestors of mammals did.
challenging.against: Her branch has been evolving for exactly as long as ours. She has features no early mammal had, such as a bill that senses electric signals, and venom spurs on the males.
challenging.context: This card is about whether an animal with old features is an old kind of animal.

challenging.for: The early relatives of mammals had scaly-looking bodies and sprawling legs, and were once called 'mammal-like reptiles'.
challenging.against: The line leading to mammals and the line leading to lizards, crocodiles and birds split about 320 million years ago, from early animals with an amnion. Those shared ancestors were not lizards, snakes, turtles or crocodiles. Neither line came from the other.
challenging.context: This card is about where the mammal branch joins the family tree.

challenging.who: Most scientists who name groups by whole branches
challenging.for: The branch that holds lizards, turtles and crocodiles also holds the dinosaurs, and birds are dinosaurs. A crocodile is a closer relative of a crow than of a lizard.
challenging.against: In everyday speech 'reptile' means a scaly animal who takes warmth from outside. Birds have feathers and make their own heat, so the everyday word does not fit them.
challenging.context: This card is about what the word 'reptile' should cover.

challenging.claim: Evolution climbs a ladder from fish up to humans.
challenging.who: A very old picture, still common in cartoons
challenging.for: Fish came first, and humans are recent.
challenging.against: The family tree is a branching tree with no top. Most vertebrates alive today are fish. Fish did not stop evolving when one branch moved onto land.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the family tree has a top.

challenging.claim: Lungs evolved from the swim bladders of fish.
challenging.for: A swim bladder and a lung are both bags of gas, and they grow from the same part of the gut.
challenging.against: Bichirs and lungfish, on two early branches, both have lungs. So the shared ancestor of bony fish probably had lungs, and the swim bladder is the later change.
challenging.context: This card is about which came first, the lung or the swim bladder.

big_questions.q: Go back from mother to mother for 400 million years and you reach a fish. Was there ever a mother who was a fish with a daughter who was not?
big_questions.hint: Every daughter was almost exactly like her mother. So where could a line between two groups go?

big_questions.q: The groups look separate because the in-between animals died out. If they were all alive, could we still sort vertebrates into five groups?
big_questions.hint: Think of the colours of a rainbow. Where does green stop and blue begin?

big_questions.q: A platypus lays eggs and gives milk. Does she break the rule for mammals, or was the rule too simple?
big_questions.hint: Who made the rule, and which animals had they seen when they made it?

big_questions.q: Your body carries broken instructions for making egg yolk. What does that tell you about who you are?
big_questions.hint: How far back does your own family go?

big_questions.q: If every vertebrate is your relative, does that change how you think about the fish on a plate or the crow on the wall?
big_questions.hint: There is no one right answer. People who know the same facts decide differently.

big_questions.q: Scientists named the groups before they knew about evolution. When we learn something new, should old names change?
big_questions.hint: Think of the word 'reptile'. What is gained and what is lost if we change what it means?

story.title: The Fish in the Brass Pot
story.note: A made-up story. Yazhini, Kathir, Thangam Akka, the village and the events are imagined. The fish is real. The murrel, called viral in Tamil, lives in tanks and paddy fields across India, burrows into the mud when the water dries, and must come to the surface to breathe air. Sharing out the fish of a drying tank is a real custom in many Tamil villages.
text: By the middle of May the big tank at the edge of the village was a small one. The water had drawn back from the stone steps, then from the reeds, and at last from everything but a brown pool in the middle, no deeper than Yazhini's knees.

That was the day the whole village came to fish. It happened every year when the tank ran low. People walked in with baskets and old saris and their bare hands, and whatever they caught was shared out by the steps.
Yazhini was ten, and she did not like the fishing day. She liked the fish. She stood at the edge with her small brother Kathir and watched the pool.

The carp were in trouble before anyone touched them. They hung just under the surface in a crowd, all facing up, their mouths opening and closing at the top of the water. Some had already turned on their sides.
'They are thirsty,' said Kathir.
'They are in water,' said Yazhini. 'How can they be thirsty?' But she had no better word for it.
Away from the pool the mud had dried into plates with curled edges. Yazhini walked out over it, because nobody else was looking there. Near a clump of dead reeds one of the plates moved.

She knelt down. Under the crust the mud was still soft, and in the soft mud lay a fish as long as her arm, dark and round as a rolling pin, with a flat head like a snake's. There was not a cupful of water round her. Her gill covers lifted and fell. She looked at Yazhini with a small bright eye.
'Viral,' said Thangam Akka, who sold fish in the market and had come up behind her with a basket. 'A big one. She has been sitting in there a week, I would say. Shall I take her?'
'No,' said Yazhini. 'I found her. I am going to keep her until it rains.'
Thangam Akka laughed, but she did not argue. She wrapped the fish in a wet cloth for her and went back to the pool.

At home Yazhini took the tall brass pot from behind the kitchen door, the one with the narrow neck that was used only at Pongal. She carried it to the well and filled it. Then she thought of how dry the fish had been in that mud, and she went on pouring until the water stood right at the lip.
She slid the fish in. The fish went down into the dark and turned once.
'The cat,' said Kathir.

The cat was already on the wall, looking interested. Yazhini fetched a steel plate and pressed it down on the mouth of the pot. It fitted well. A little water ran over the sides. She put a stone on top.
'There,' she said. 'All the water she wants, and nobody can get at her.'
They sat down in the shade to guard the pot.
After a while there was a knock from inside. It was soft, like a knuckle on a door. Then another.
'She wants to come out,' said Kathir.
'She does not know she is safe yet,' said Yazhini.

The knocking came again, four or five times, harder. The stone shifted on the plate. Then there was a long quiet. Yazhini lifted the edge of the plate a finger's width and looked in. The fish was lying just under the brass, on her side, with her mouth pressed against the plate.

Yazhini's stomach turned over. She had seen fish lie like that an hour ago. The carp in the pool had hung at the top with their mouths at the surface, in all that water. And this one had lain a week in mud with no water at all, and her eye had been bright.

She thought about the tank in January, when it was full. She used to sit on the steps and count the rings. A ring would open on the still water, far out, with a small sound like a drop falling. Then nothing for a few minutes. Then another ring in nearly the same place. Her grandmother had told her it was the viral coming up. Yazhini had never asked what the viral came up for.
'Take the stone off,' she said.

She pulled the plate away, put both arms round the pot, and tipped it until water poured over her feet. She tipped out a good three tumblers. Now there was a hand's width of air in the neck of the pot.

For a moment the fish did not move. Then she righted herself, rose, and put her mouth through the surface. There was a small sound like a drop falling. A bubble slid out from under her gill cover. She sank back down into the dark.
Kathir looked at his sister.
'She was not trying to get out,' said Yazhini. 'She was trying to get up. She breathes it. The same as us.'
'A fish?'
'This fish.'
They watched. In a little while the fish came up again, took her mouthful, and went down.

The cat was still on the wall. Yazhini went into the kitchen and came back with the net bag the onions came in. She stretched it over the mouth of the pot and tied it round the neck with string. The cat could look. The air could go in.
That evening Thangam Akka came by with their share of the carp. She looked through the net at the dark shape turning in the pot and raised her eyebrows.
'Still alive? You have not drowned her, then. People do.'
'I nearly did,' said Yazhini.
The rain came eleven days later, in the night. In the morning the pool in the tank had spread back as far as the reeds. Yazhini and Kathir carried the pot down between them and tipped it at the edge.
The fish slid out and was gone. They waited. Far out on the brown water, a ring opened.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the carp and the murrel are both fish, but they get their oxygen in different ways. The carp have gills only. In a warm, shrinking pool the water holds very little oxygen, so they gasp at the surface even though they are surrounded by water. The murrel has gills and an air chamber above them, and she depends on gulping air. That is why she could live for a week in damp mud. It is also why a pot filled to the brim and shut with a plate nearly killed her. She could not reach the air. Yazhini works this out from what she saw: which fish was dying in water, which was alive without it, and the rings on the tank.
ask: The carp were in water and in trouble. The murrel was in mud and well. What does that tell you about how each one gets oxygen?
Why did filling the pot to the brim and covering it put the murrel in danger?
What had Yazhini seen on the full tank in January that helped her work it out?
Why was the net bag a better cover than the steel plate?
If you kept a fish, what would you want to find out about her first?

games.title: Sure or Surprised? Twenty true or false cards
games.context: You will find out which surprising animal facts are really true. This is a card game about the five groups of vertebrates. Each card makes a claim. You say whether it is true or false, and you bet beans on how sure you are.

printables.title: 20 claim cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.b: FALSE. Birds are a branch of the dinosaurs. The crow outside is a living dinosaur.
FALSE. The platypus and the four echidnas are mammals, and they lay eggs.
TRUE. A murrel or a climbing perch must gulp air. Held under water with no way up, she can drown.

items.f: Some snakes give birth to live young.
items.b: TRUE. The Russell's viper, the saw-scaled viper and the sand boa do. Cobras and rat snakes lay eggs.

items.f: A crocodile is a closer relative of a lizard than of a crow.
items.b: FALSE. Crocodiles are the closest living relatives of birds. Lizards branched off earlier.

items.f: The ancestors of whales walked on four legs.
items.b: TRUE. Indohyus, a fox-sized hoofed animal from Kashmir, was a close relative of the first whales.

items.f: Lungs first appeared in animals who lived on land.
items.b: FALSE. Lungs first appeared in fish, more than 400 million years ago.

items.f: The first animals with fingers had five on each hand.
items.b: FALSE. Acanthostega had eight fingers on each hand.

items.f: A platypus mother has no teats.
items.b: TRUE. Her milk comes out through openings in the skin, and the babies take it from her fur.

items.f: Your DNA holds broken instructions for making egg yolk.
items.b: TRUE. Our egg-laying ancestors needed them. In us they no longer work.

items.f: Bats are close relatives of birds, because both fly.
items.b: FALSE. Bats are mammals. Wings arose separately in bats and in birds.

items.f: Milk evolved before mammals stopped laying eggs.
items.b: TRUE. The egg-laying platypus makes milk, and the milk genes are shared by all mammals.

items.f: The platypus stopped evolving millions of years ago.
items.b: FALSE. Her branch gained new features, such as a bill that senses electric signals.

items.f: A snake is a tetrapod, a four-limbed animal.
items.b: TRUE. Her ancestors were lizards with four legs. The group is named for the ancestors.

items.f: Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen than cold water.
items.b: FALSE. Warm water holds less. That is why fish gasp in warm, shallow ponds.
TRUE. Before birth, at about five to eight weeks, you had a small tail. Your tailbone is what is left.

items.f: Most kinds of vertebrate alive today are mammals.
items.b: FALSE. About half of all kinds of vertebrate are fish.

items.f: A fish's swim bladder is a changed lung.
items.b: TRUE. Most scientists think the first bony fish had lungs, and the swim bladder came from them.

items.f: A frog's closest relative can live on a faraway island.
items.b: TRUE. The purple frog of the Western Ghats has her closest relatives on the Seychelles islands.

items.f: A mother crocodile leaves her eggs and never returns.
items.b: FALSE. She guards the nest and answers her young when they call from inside the eggs.

rules: Each player starts with 20 beans, such as rajma or groundnuts. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, claim side up.
One player reads the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
Every player says 'true' or 'false' and puts 1, 2 or 3 beans in front of them. One bean means 'I am guessing'. Three beans means 'I am very sure'.
Turn the card over and read the back.
If you were right, take your beans back, and take the same number again from the spare beans. If you were wrong, your beans go to the spare beans.
After 20 cards, the player with the most beans wins.
Playing alone: play the same way against the pile. Try to end with more than 40 beans. Play again a week later and beat your score.

setup.caption: 1. Give each player 20 beans. Put the cards in a pile, claim side up.

setup.art: A child holding up two fingers and pushing two beans forward while a parent reads from a card.
setup.caption: 2. Say true or false. Bet 1, 2 or 3 beans on how sure you are.

setup.art: A card turned over on the table showing the word FALSE and a short sentence, with beans being collected.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Win or lose your beans.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Count 20 beans for each player and keep a katori of spare beans. 3. Shuffle the cards and pile them claim side up.
flow.say: Each card makes a claim about animals with a backbone. Some are true and some are false. You bet beans on how sure you are.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Count 20 beans for yourself. Pile the cards with the claims facing up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sure or Surprised? Here you get the cards and the beans ready.

flow.do: 1. Read the top claim aloud. 2. Each player says true or false and bets 1, 2 or 3 beans. 3. Ask one player for a reason. 4. Turn the card and read the back. 5. Pay out or collect the beans.
flow.say: True or false? How sure are you? Tell me one reason before we turn the card.
flow.kid: Read the claim. Say true or false. Bet your beans. Then turn the card over.

ask.q: You bet three beans and you were wrong. What made you so sure?
good: I thought all mammals are born alive, because all the ones I know are.
I had only seen snakes' eggs in books.

flow.parent: The most useful cards are the ones your child was very sure of and got wrong. Ask what made them sure. Usually the rule they learnt was true of the animals they had met, and not of all animals.
flow.context: This is the main part of Sure or Surprised? Here you bet on each claim and then check it.

flow.do: 1. Count the beans. 2. Spread out the cards you got wrong, answer side up. 3. Choose the one that surprised you most and say why it is true or false.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Explain it to me as if I had never heard it.
flow.kid: Count your beans. Find the card that surprised you most. Explain it to someone.

check.q: Which of these claims is true?
options: Every mammal is born alive
Some snakes bear live young
Lungs first appeared on land
check.why: Russell's vipers, saw-scaled vipers and sand boas bear live young. The platypus is a mammal who lays eggs, and lungs first appeared in fish. Choosing the first option usually means thinking only of the mammals we see every day.

flow.context: This is the last step of Sure or Surprised? Here you count the beans and explain the claim that surprised you most.

games.title: Closest Cousins: which two are nearest on the family tree?
games.context: You will find out which animals are really close relatives. This is a card game about the family tree of vertebrates. Three animals are turned up, and you pick the two who are the closest relatives. The back of each card gives the animal's place on the tree, so you can check.

rules: Shuffle the 18 cards and put them in a pile, name side up.
Turn up the top three cards and lay them in a row, name side up.
On the count of three, every player points to the two animals they think are the closest relatives.
Turn the three cards over. Read each address from the left. The two animals whose addresses stay the same for the most steps are the closest relatives.
Every player who pointed to that pair scores 1 point. If all three addresses stay the same for equally many steps, every pair is right.
Put the three cards aside and turn up three more. After six rounds, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: play the six rounds and score yourself out of 6. Shuffle and play again.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards. 2. Read one back together, such as the crow's. 3. Explain that each step is a fork in the family tree. 4. Shuffle and pile the cards name side up.
flow.say: The back of each card is the animal's address on the family tree. Each step is a fork where the family split.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the back of one card. Each step is a fork in the tree.
flow.parent: The addresses are simplified. Many forks are left out, but the order of the forks that are shown is the order scientists agree on.
flow.context: This is the first step of Closest Cousins. Here you get the cards ready and learn to read an address.

flow.do: 1. Turn up three cards. 2. Count to three, and everyone points to two animals. 3. Ask one player for a reason. 4. Turn the cards and compare the addresses step by step. 5. Give the points. 6. Play six rounds.
flow.say: Which two are the closest relatives? Do not go by where they live or what shape they are. Think about their features.
flow.kid: Turn up three cards. Point to the two closest relatives. Turn the cards and check.

ask.q: A dolphin, a whale shark and a fruit bat are turned up. Which two are closest, and why?
good: The dolphin and the bat, because both are mammals with a placenta.
The dolphin looks like the shark only because both swim fast.

flow.parent: Expect your child to pair animals by shape or by home at first, such as the dolphin with the shark. Let the addresses show the answer. Then ask which features the true pair shares.
flow.context: This is the main part of Closest Cousins. Here you pick the two closest relatives out of three animals, six times.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out the crocodile, the gecko and the crow. 3. Ask which two are closest, and check with the addresses. 4. Ask why this one fools people.
flow.say: Here are a crocodile, a gecko and a crow. Which two are closest? Why does this one fool nearly everybody?
flow.kid: Lay out the crocodile, the gecko and the crow. Think about their features, then check the backs.

check.q: Which two of these are the closest relatives?
options: Mugger crocodile and house gecko
Mugger crocodile and house crow
House gecko and house crow
check.why: The crocodile and the crow share the fork 'crocodiles and dinosaurs', which the gecko is not on. Choosing the crocodile and the gecko usually means going by scales and shape. Those are old features that all three branches started with, and birds changed theirs.

flow.context: This is the last step of Closest Cousins. Here you count the points and look at the crocodile, the gecko and the crow.

experiments.title: Air in Water: why would a fish ever need to breathe air?
experiments.context: You will find out why a fish in a warm pond can struggle to breathe. Fish take oxygen from the air that is dissolved in water. In this experiment you compare three tumblers of water: one that starts cold, one at room warmth, and one that was boiled. You watch for bubbles of air coming out as they stand in a warm place.
experiments.question: Three tumblers of water look exactly the same. One was kept in the fridge, one stood on the kitchen counter, and one was boiled and cooled. When all three stand in a warm place for an hour, in which one will the most bubbles of air appear on the glass?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which tumbler will show the most bubbles after an hour in a warm place: the cold water, the room-warm water or the boiled water? Which will show the fewest? Write your guess and your reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only what happened to the water before the test. Use the same drinking water for all three. Use three tumblers of the same size and shape, filled to the same height. Stand them side by side in the same warm place for the same time. Count bubbles on the inside of the glass only, and count each tumbler at the same three times.

materials.item: clear glass tumblers of the same size and shape
clean bottles with caps, 1 litre or smaller
drinking water, about 1 litre
a small pot with a lid, and a stove
a fridge
three paper slips marked COLD, ROOM and BOILED
a sunny window sill or another warm place
a clock or phone timer, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water and handles the hot pot. Let the boiled water cool completely before your child touches it.

schedule.what: In the morning, get the three waters ready: one bottle in the fridge, one on the counter, and one pot of boiled water cooling under a lid. Leave them for at least 3 hours.
In the afternoon, pour the three tumblers, stand them in a warm place, and count the bubbles at 20, 40 and 60 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three tumblers. If there are more than 30 bubbles, write 'more than 30'. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
