setup.caption: 1. Get three waters ready: one cold, one at room warmth, one boiled and cooled. Wait 3 hours.

setup.art: Three identical glass tumblers filled to the same height, each standing on a paper slip marked COLD, ROOM or BOILED.
setup.caption: 2. Pour one tumbler of each, to the same height.

setup.art: The three tumblers side by side on a sunny window sill with a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Stand all three in the same warm place.

setup.art: A close view of the inside wall of a glass tumbler covered with many small silver bubbles, with a child's finger pointing and counting.
setup.caption: 4. Count the bubbles on the inside of each glass at 20, 40 and 60 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Half-fill two bottles with drinking water and cap them. 2. Shake each bottle hard for 30 seconds. 3. Put one bottle in the fridge and leave the other on the counter. 4. A grown-up boils two tumblers of water in the pot for 5 minutes. 5. Put the lid on the pot and leave it to cool. 6. Do not stir or shake the boiled water.
flow.say: We are making three kinds of water that look the same. One will be cold, one room-warm, and one boiled. Shaking mixes air into the water.
flow.kid: Half-fill two bottles and shake them hard. Put one in the fridge. A grown-up boils the third water.
flow.parent: Shaking a half-full bottle lets the water take in as much air as it can hold at that temperature. Boiling drives nearly all the dissolved air out, and the lid slows its return.
flow.wait: Leave all three for at least 3 hours, until the boiled water is as cool as the room.
flow.context: This is the first step of Air in Water. Here you prepare cold water, room-warm water and boiled water, a few hours before the test.

flow.do: 1. Shake the cold bottle again for 30 seconds and put it back in the fridge for 2 minutes. 2. Meanwhile, read the question aloud. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: All three waters will warm up at the window. Which glass will show the most bubbles, and which the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which tumbler will show the most bubbles? Which the fewest? Write your guess.

good: The boiled one, because boiling makes bubbles.
The cold one, because something changes when it warms up.
All the same, because it is the same water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children pick the boiled water, because they have seen bubbles in a boiling pot. The two minutes of rest lets the tiny shaken bubbles rise out of the cold water.
flow.context: This step of Air in Water is for guessing. You guess before any water is poured.

flow.do: 1. Put the three paper slips on the window sill. 2. Pour cold water gently into the first tumbler, to two finger-widths below the rim. 3. Pour room-warm water into the second, to the same height. 4. Pour boiled water into the third, slowly, down the side of the glass. 5. Check that no glass has bubbles on it yet. 6. Note the time.
flow.say: Pour gently, so that we do not mix in new air. Look closely. Is there any bubble on any glass now?
flow.kid: Pour each water gently into a tumbler. Fill them to the same height. Stand them in the warm place.
flow.parent: If a few bubbles cling to a glass right after pouring, tap the glass to free them, and start the clock after that.
flow.wait: Leave the tumblers for 20 minutes. Do not move them.
flow.context: This is the pouring step of Air in Water. Here you fill three tumblers to the same height and stand them in a warm place.

flow.do: 1. After 20 minutes, look at the inside wall of each glass without moving it. 2. Count the bubbles on each and write the numbers. 3. Count again at 40 minutes and at 60 minutes.
flow.say: Do not lift the glasses. Count the bubbles on the inside of each one. Which glass has changed most since we poured?
flow.kid: Count the bubbles inside each glass. Write the numbers. Count again at 40 and 60 minutes.

ask.q: Nothing was added to the cold water. So where did the bubbles come from?
good: They were inside the water already.
Air was hidden in the water and came out when it warmed.

flow.parent: Expect many small bubbles in the cold-water glass by 40 minutes, a few or none in the room-warm glass, and none in the boiled glass. If the cold glass has very few after an hour, wait one more hour, or repeat with an older glass. Bubbles start most easily on tiny scratches.
flow.context: This is the counting step of Air in Water. Here you count the bubbles on each glass at 20, 40 and 60 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences: what they thought, what they saw, and why. 2. Ask which glass of water held the most dissolved air at the start. 3. Ask what this means for a fish in a warm, shallow pond in May. 4. Only then read the card 'Why some fish breathe air' together.
flow.say: Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why it happened. Then think of a shallow pond on a hot day. What is hard for a fish there?
flow.kid: Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why. What is hard for a fish in a warm pond?

ask.q: The cold water lost air as it warmed. What does that tell you about warm water?
good: Warm water cannot hold as much air as cold water.
The extra air had to come out.

ask.q: The boiled water showed no bubbles. Does it have a lot of air or very little?
good: Very little, because boiling drove the air out.
You cannot tell by looking, because all three looked the same.

flow.parent: The bubbles are air, which is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. We counted bubbles, and we did not measure oxygen itself. The test shows that water holds dissolved air, and that warm water holds less of it than cold water.

check.q: Cold water stands in a warm place, and bubbles appear on the glass. What are they?
options: Dissolved air leaving the warming water
Air leaking in through the glass
Water turning into steam
check.why: Cold water holds more dissolved air than warm water. As the water warmed, the extra air came out as bubbles. Choosing 'steam' usually means thinking of the bubbles in a boiling pot. Water does not turn to steam at room warmth, and steam bubbles rise and burst at once.

flow.context: This is the last step of Air in Water. Here you explain your results and link them to fish in a warm pond.

experiments.title: Lap or Suck: how much does a teat help a baby drink?
experiments.context: You will find out how much a teat helps a baby drink. A platypus mother has no teats. Her milk comes out through her skin, and her babies take it from her fur. In this experiment you drink water in three ways, from a plate, from a wet cloth and through a straw, and measure how much you get each time.
experiments.question: You have 20 seconds to drink 4 tablespoons of water. How much will you get by lapping from a flat plate, by taking it from a wet cloth, and by sucking through a straw? And how much is spilt or left behind each way?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the three ways in order, from the one that gives you the most water in 20 seconds to the one that gives you the least. Guess how many tablespoons will be left each way. Write your guess and your reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the way of drinking. Use the same person, the same 4 tablespoons of water and the same 20 seconds each time. Do not lift the plate or the cloth with your hands. Do each way twice and find the mean, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a flat steel plate with a rim
a clean cotton handkerchief or a piece of clean cotton cloth
a drinking straw
a tablespoon and two steel tumblers
drinking water, about half a litre
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a towel, a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Drink 4 tablespoons of water in three ways, twice each, and measure what is left each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three ways. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A flat steel plate on a table with a shallow pool of water in the middle, a tablespoon beside it and a phone showing a timer.
setup.caption: 1. Put 4 tablespoons of water on the plate.

setup.art: A child with hands behind her back bending over the plate and lapping the water with her tongue, while a grown-up watches the timer.
setup.caption: 2. Way one: lap from the plate for 20 seconds. No hands.

setup.art: The same plate with a folded cotton cloth lying in it, soaked with water, and the child bending to take water from the cloth.
setup.caption: 3. Way two: take the water from a soaked cloth. No hands.

setup.art: A steel tumbler holding a little water with a straw in it, and the child drinking through the straw.
setup.caption: 4. Way three: suck through a straw from a tumbler.

setup.art: A grown-up tipping the plate into a tumbler and then spooning the water out one tablespoon at a time.
setup.caption: 5. Each time, measure what is left with the tablespoon.

flow.do: 1. Wash your hands, the plate, the cloth, the spoon and the tumblers. 2. Lay the towel on the table and put the plate on it. 3. Tell your child how a platypus baby feeds. 4. Show the three ways of drinking.
flow.say: A platypus mother has no teats. Milk comes out of her skin onto her fur, and her babies take it from there. We will try three ways of drinking.
flow.kid: Wash your hands and the plate. Put the plate on a towel. You will drink in three ways.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lap or Suck. Here you set up a plate, a cloth and a straw to model three ways a baby mammal might drink.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put the three ways in order. 2. Ask how many tablespoons will be left each time. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write it all down.
flow.say: Plate, wet cloth or straw. Which gives you the most water in 20 seconds? How much will be left each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which way gives you the most water? Put the three in order. Say why. Write it down.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children pick the straw. The interesting part is how big the difference is, and where the lost water goes.
flow.context: This step of Lap or Suck is for guessing. You guess before anyone drinks.

flow.do: 1. Measure 4 tablespoons of water onto the plate. 2. Your child puts their hands behind their back. 3. Say 'go' and time 20 seconds of lapping. 4. Tip what is left into an empty tumbler. 5. Spoon it back out and count the tablespoons, to the nearest half. 6. Wipe the plate and do it once more.
flow.say: This is way one. Lap the water straight from the plate, like a cat. You have 20 seconds, and no hands.
flow.kid: Lap the water from the plate for 20 seconds. No hands. Then measure what is left.
flow.parent: Count any water that splashed onto the towel as lost. Note it beside the result.
flow.context: This is way one of Lap or Suck. Here you lap water from a flat plate and measure what is left.

flow.do: 1. Fold the cloth in four and lay it in the plate. 2. Pour 4 tablespoons of water slowly onto the cloth. 3. Time 20 seconds while your child takes water from the cloth, with no hands. 4. Squeeze the cloth into the empty tumbler and tip in any water from the plate. 5. Count the tablespoons left. 6. Do it once more.
flow.say: This is way two. The cloth is the mother's fur, wet with milk. Get what you can from it in 20 seconds.
flow.kid: Take water from the wet cloth for 20 seconds. No hands. Squeeze out what is left and measure it.
flow.parent: Squeezing never gets all the water out of the cloth. So the amount left will read a little low, and the amount drunk a little high. Say this when you look at the results.
flow.context: This is way two of Lap or Suck. Here you take water from a soaked cloth, the way a platypus baby takes milk from fur.

flow.do: 1. Measure 4 tablespoons of water into a tumbler. 2. Put in the straw. 3. Time 20 seconds of sucking, or stop the clock when the water is gone. 4. Count any tablespoons left. 5. Do it once more.
flow.say: This is way three. The straw is a teat. Suck for 20 seconds, or until the water is gone. I will time you.
flow.kid: Suck the water through the straw. Stop at 20 seconds or when it is gone. Measure what is left.
flow.parent: The water will probably be gone in well under 20 seconds. Write down how many seconds it took.
flow.context: This is way three of Lap or Suck. Here you suck water through a straw, the way most baby mammals suck from a teat.

flow.do: 1. For each way, add the two results and halve the total to find the average left. 2. Take the average left from 4 to find the average drunk. 3. Ask your child for the three sentences. 4. Ask what our model leaves out. 5. Then read the card 'Mammals who lay eggs' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought, what you saw and why. Then tell me one way that you and a straw differ from a platypus baby and her mother.
flow.kid: Work out the average left for each way. Say what you thought and what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Platypus babies grow well with no teat. So what might a teat add?
good: The baby can drink faster.
Less milk is spilt or left in the fur.
The baby can hold on while the mother moves.

ask.q: What does our model leave out?
good: A platypus baby's mouth is shaped for this, and mine is not.
The mother's fur and skin are not a handkerchief.
Milk is thicker than water.

flow.parent: This is a model, so it can show one thing only: a tube that fits the mouth wastes less and delivers faster. Nobody knows for certain why teats evolved. The model fits one sensible idea, and it does not prove it.

check.q: A platypus has milk but no teats. What does this tell us about the history of mammals?
options: Milk evolved before teats did
The platypus lost her teats recently
Platypus babies do not need milk
check.why: The platypus's branch split off after milk had evolved and before teats had. So she shows the earlier way of giving milk. Choosing 'lost her teats' usually means assuming that every mammal started with all the mammal features.

flow.context: This is the last step of Lap or Suck. Here you work out the means and say what the model shows and what it leaves out.

activities.title: The Feature Ladder: which features came first?
activities.context: In this activity you make a table of seven vertebrates and six features, and tick who has what. The ticks form steps, and the steps show the order in which the features arrived in the history of animals.

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a ruler and a pencil
a colour pencil

activities.record: Keep the table. Under it write two sentences: which came first, lungs or legs, and which came first, milk or birth without an egg. Say which animal in your table shows each answer.

setup.art: A sheet of paper ruled into a table with seven rows labelled rohu, lungfish, frog, crocodile, pigeon, platypus and cow, and six columns labelled backbone, lungs, four limbs, amnion, fur and milk, born alive.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with seven animals down the side and six features along the top.

setup.art: The same table with ticks filled in, forming a staircase shape from one tick for the rohu to six ticks for the cow.
setup.caption: 2. Tick each feature an animal has. Count the ticks in each row.

setup.art: A child's pencil circling two rows of the table: the lungfish row with ticks under backbone and lungs only, and the platypus row with a tick under fur and milk but none under born alive.
setup.caption: 3. Find the two rows that settle the questions: the lungfish and the platypus.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with seven rows and six columns. 2. Write the animals down the side: rohu, lungfish, frog, crocodile, pigeon, platypus, cow. 3. Write the features along the top: backbone, lungs, four limbs, amnion, fur and milk, born alive. 4. Ask the two questions below and write the guesses.
flow.say: Before we fill this in, guess. Which came first in history, lungs or legs? Which came first, milk or babies born without an egg? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the table. Then guess. Lungs or legs first? Milk or birth first? Say why.
flow.parent: An amnion is the bag of water that a baby reptile, bird or mammal grows in. Explain the word before you start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Feature Ladder. Here you draw the table and guess which features came first.

flow.do: 1. Read out each fact and let your child put the ticks. 2. The rohu, a carp, has a backbone only. 3. The lungfish has a backbone and lungs. 4. The frog has a backbone, lungs and four limbs. 5. The crocodile has those three and grows in an amnion, the bag of fluid around a baby inside the egg. 6. The pigeon has the same four as the crocodile. Her wings are her front limbs. 7. The platypus has those four, and fur and milk. She lays eggs. 8. The cow has those five, and is born alive.
flow.say: I will read what each animal has. You put the ticks. Tell me if anything surprises you as we go.
flow.kid: Listen to what each animal has. Tick each feature in the table.
flow.parent: The rohu's swim bladder is a changed lung, so leave her lung box empty and tell your child why afterwards. The pigeon also has feathers, which no other animal in the table has. Write 'feathers' beside her row.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Feature Ladder. Here you tick which of six features each of seven animals has.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks in each row and write the number at the end. 2. Look at the ticks from the top row to the bottom row. 3. Look at the shape the ticks make. 4. Find the animal who has lungs and no limbs. 5. Find the animal who has milk and is not born alive.
flow.say: Look at the shape. What do you notice? Now use the table to answer your two guesses. Which rows give the answers?
flow.kid: Count the ticks in each row. Who has lungs but no limbs? Who has milk but lays eggs?

ask.q: How does the table show that lungs came before legs?
good: The lungfish has lungs and no legs, and nobody has legs without lungs.
Every animal with four limbs also has lungs.

flow.parent: The rows should hold 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5 and 6 ticks. The shading makes a staircase. No animal has a later feature without all the earlier ones.
flow.context: This step of the Feature Ladder is for reading the table. Here you find the order in which the features arrived.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether the cow is 'more evolved' than the rohu, and listen. 2. Explain that all seven animals are alive today. 3. Ask what the steps really show. 4. Add yourself to the table and tick your own features.
flow.say: Is the cow a better animal than the rohu because she has more ticks? All seven are alive now. So what do the steps show?
flow.kid: Is the cow better than the rohu? Add yourself to the table.

ask.q: What do the steps show, if not better and worse?
good: The order in which the features first appeared.
Where each animal's branch split off from ours.

flow.parent: We chose features on the line that leads to the cow, so the cow gets the most ticks. If we had chosen features of the rohu's own branch, such as fan fins and a swim bladder, the rohu would get the most.

check.q: The platypus has fur and milk and lays eggs. What does this show?
options: Milk evolved before birth without an egg
The platypus is half bird
Eggs evolved after milk
check.why: Her branch split off after milk evolved and before mammals stopped laying eggs. So milk is the older feature of the two. Choosing 'half bird' usually means treating each group's features as one set that cannot be split up.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Feature Ladder. Here you ask what the steps show, and add yourself to the table.

activities.title: Old Parts in Your Body: goosebumps, a tailbone and a wrist tendon
activities.context: You will find out why you get goosebumps. Bodies keep small leftovers of parts that did more in their ancestors. In this activity you find three such leftovers in your own body, and count how many people at home have one of them.

materials.item: an ice cube or a cloth dipped in cold water
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw your forearm with goosebumps, or tell a grown-up what you saw. Then make a tally: how many people at home have the wrist tendon in both wrists, in one wrist, or in neither.

setup.art: A child holding an ice cube against the inside of her forearm and looking closely at the fine hairs standing up on small bumps.
setup.caption: 1. Cool your forearm and watch the small hairs stand up.

setup.art: A child sitting on the floor with one finger at the very bottom of her backbone.
setup.caption: 2. Feel the end of your backbone. That is your tailbone.

setup.art: A hand held palm up with the thumb touching the little finger and the wrist bent slightly, and a thin cord standing out in the middle of the wrist.
setup.caption: 3. Touch your thumb to your little finger and bend your wrist a little. Look for a cord in the middle of the wrist.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ice cube on the inside of your child's forearm for 20 seconds. 2. Take it away and look at the skin closely, in good light. 3. Ask what the small hairs are doing. 4. Ask what the same thing would do for a cat or a monkey.
flow.say: Look at the tiny hairs. What are they doing? A small muscle is pulling each one upright. What would that do for an animal with thick fur?
flow.kid: Cool your forearm with ice. Look at the tiny hairs. What are they doing?

ask.q: Why would standing hair help a furry animal who is cold?
good: Fluffed fur holds more air, and the air keeps warmth in.
A cat looks bigger with her fur up.

flow.parent: Goosebumps are a leftover of fur-raising. The muscles still work, but our body hair is too thin to hold a layer of warm air.
flow.context: This is the first step of Old Parts in Your Body. Here you make goosebumps and ask what they once did.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to run a finger down the middle of their back to the very end of the backbone. 2. Explain that the last small bones are the tailbone. 3. Tell them that they had a small tail before they were born.
flow.say: Follow your backbone down to the very end. Those last small bones are your tailbone. What do you think they are left over from?
flow.kid: Follow your backbone down to the end. That is your tailbone. What is it left over from?
flow.parent: The tailbone is three to five small bones joined together. It still has a use: muscles attach to it. A leftover part can keep a small job.
flow.context: This step of Old Parts in Your Body is about the tailbone, the leftover of a tail.

flow.do: 1. Hold one hand palm up. 2. Touch the thumb to the little finger and bend the wrist slightly towards you. 3. Look for a thin cord standing up in the middle of the wrist. 4. Test both wrists. 5. Test everyone at home and tally: both wrists, one wrist or neither.
flow.say: Do you see a cord in the middle of your wrist? Some people have it and some do not. Let's test everyone at home and count.
flow.kid: Touch thumb to little finger. Bend your wrist a little. Do you see a cord? Test both wrists. Test your family.
flow.parent: The cord is the tendon of a muscle called the palmaris longus. People without it grip just as well. It is thought to be a leftover from ancestors who climbed with their arms. If nobody at home lacks it, that is a normal result for a small group.
flow.context: This step of Old Parts in Your Body is a small survey. Here you find out who at home has a wrist tendon that many people lack.

flow.do: 1. Try to wiggle your ears without touching them. 2. Ask who at home can. 3. Ask your child what all these leftovers have in common. 4. Ask what they tell us about our ancestors.
flow.say: We found fur muscles, a tail's end, and a climbing muscle that some of us have lost. What do they tell you about our ancestors?
flow.kid: Try to wiggle your ears. Who at home can do it?

ask.q: What do these leftovers tell us?
good: Our ancestors had thick fur and tails.
Bodies are changed from older bodies, and small parts of the old ones stay.

check.q: Why do humans get goosebumps when they are cold?
options: Small muscles raise hairs that were once thick fur
The skin shrinks in the cold
Cold air gets under the skin
check.why: A tiny muscle at each hair pulls the hair upright. On a furry ancestor this fluffed the coat and kept warmth in. Choosing 'the skin shrinks' usually means not having looked closely at the hairs.

flow.context: This is the last step of Old Parts in Your Body. Here you say what the leftovers have in common.

activities.title: Count the Differences: reading the family tree from letters
activities.context: Scientists check the family tree by comparing DNA, which can be written as a string of four letters. In this activity you compare five made-up strings that follow the real pattern, and work out who is the closest relative of whom.

materials.item: squared paper or plain paper, and a pencil
a colour pencil

activities.record: Keep the five strings with the differences circled. Under them write the four counts. Take a photo of the slips laid out as the family tree they suggest, or draw it.

setup.art: A sheet of squared paper with five rows of fifteen letters, one letter in each square, labelled human, cow, hen, frog and carp.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the five strings, one letter in each square, one string under the other.

setup.art: The same sheet with some letters in the cow, hen, frog and carp rows circled in colour where they differ from the human row above.
setup.caption: 2. Circle every letter that differs from the human string. Count the circles in each row.

setup.art: A small hand-drawn branching tree with five tips labelled carp, frog, hen, cow and human, in that order.
setup.caption: 3. Lay out the tree on paper slips: the fewest differences means the closest relative.

flow.do: 1. Copy these five strings in rows, one letter in each square. 2. Human: GATCC ATGAC TAGGA. 3. Cow: GATCC ATGAC CGGGA. 4. Hen: GATCC AATCT TAGGA. 5. Frog: GAGAT GTGAT TAGGA. 6. Carp: CCTCC GTGAT TAATC. 7. Check each row twice against this list.
flow.say: These strings are made up, but they behave like real DNA. Before we count, guess. Which animal's string will be most like the human one?
flow.kid: Copy the five strings, one letter in each square. Guess whose string is most like the human one.
flow.parent: Real DNA strings are millions of letters long. We use 15 made-up letters, so that the counting takes minutes and the pattern is the same as the real one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Differences. Here you copy five short letter strings that stand for DNA.

flow.do: 1. Compare the cow string with the human string, square by square. 2. Circle each letter that differs. 3. Do the same for the hen, the frog and the carp. 4. Write the number of circles at the end of each row.
flow.say: Go square by square. Circle a letter only if it differs from the human letter above it. How many in each row?
flow.kid: Compare each string with the human one. Circle the letters that differ. Count the circles.
flow.parent: The counts should be: cow 2, hen 4, frog 5 and carp 7. If a count is off, check the copying first.
flow.context: This is the counting step of Count the Differences. Here you count how many letters differ between the human string and each of the others.

flow.do: 1. Put the animals in order, from fewest differences to most. 2. Write each animal's name on a paper slip. Lay the slips out as a tree. Put the human and the cow on the closest twigs. Put the carp on the farthest. 3. Compare this order with your Feature Ladder, if you made one. 4. Ask why two different methods give the same order.
flow.say: Fewest differences means the most recent shared ancestor. Lay out the tree. Is the order the same as the one we got from body features?
flow.kid: Put the animals in order by the counts. Lay out the slips as a tree. Is it the same order as the body features gave?

ask.q: Bones and letters give the same tree. Why does that matter?
good: Two different kinds of evidence agree, so the tree is probably right.
If the tree were only a guess, they would not match.

check.q: Animal A differs from you in 2 letters, and animal B in 7. What does this suggest?
options: A shares a more recent ancestor with you
B shares a more recent ancestor with you
A and B are the same kind of animal
check.why: Copying mistakes build up over time. Fewer differences means less time on separate branches, so A is the closer relative. Choosing B usually means reading a bigger number as 'more related'.

flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Differences. Here you turn the counts into a family tree and compare it with the tree from body features.

activities.title: Gulp Watch: which fish come up for air? (if there is an aquarium or a pet shop near you)
activities.context: You will find out which fish come up to breathe air. Some aquarium fish breathe air and some do not. In this activity you watch two kinds of fish for five minutes each and count how often each one comes to the surface to gulp air. You need an aquarium at home, at a friend's home or in a shop.

materials.item: an aquarium with a fighting fish or a gourami, and one with a goldfish, a guppy or a molly
a phone timer or a watch
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write the name of each fish and the number of trips to the surface in five minutes. Show or tell what the fish's mouth does at the surface.

setup.art: A child standing in front of a row of small fish tanks in a pet shop, holding a notebook, with a blue fighting fish in a small tank at eye level.
setup.caption: 1. Find a fighting fish or a gourami. Ask the shopkeeper if you may watch for a few minutes.

setup.art: A fighting fish with her mouth touching the water surface and a tiny bubble at her lips.
setup.caption: 2. Watch one fish for five minutes. Make a tally mark each time she gulps at the surface.

setup.art: A goldfish swimming in the middle of a tank with a stream of bubbles rising from an air stone beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Watch a goldfish, a guppy or a molly for five minutes in the same way.

flow.do: 1. Find a fighting fish or a gourami in a tank. 2. Find a goldfish, a guppy or a molly in another tank. 3. Ask your child which fish will come to the surface more often, and why. 4. Look for a bubbling air stone or pump in each tank.
flow.say: Some fish can breathe air from the surface. Which of these two will come up for air more often? Why?
flow.kid: Find a fighting fish and a goldfish. Which will come up for air more often? Say why.
flow.parent: Fighting fish and gouramis are relatives of the climbing perch and breathe air. Shops often keep fighting fish in small bowls with no air pump, which they can survive because they gulp air.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gulp Watch. Here you choose two kinds of aquarium fish and guess which one breathes air.

flow.do: 1. Choose one fighting fish or gourami and watch only her. 2. Time five minutes. 3. Make a tally mark each time she touches the surface with her mouth. 4. Then watch one goldfish, guppy or molly for five minutes in the same way.
flow.say: Keep your eyes on one fish. Make a mark each time her mouth touches the surface. I will tell you when five minutes are up.
flow.kid: Watch one fish for five minutes. Mark each trip to the surface. Then watch the other kind.
flow.parent: A fighting fish usually comes up every few minutes, and more often in warm water. A healthy goldfish in a tank with an air pump rarely gulps at the surface. If she does it often, the water is short of oxygen.
flow.context: This is the watching step of Gulp Watch. Here you count trips to the surface for two kinds of fish.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two tallies. 2. Ask what the air pump in a goldfish tank is for. 3. Ask why a fighting fish can live in a bowl without one.
flow.say: What did you count? What is the bubbling pump in the goldfish tank for? Why can the fighting fish manage without one?
flow.kid: Compare your two counts. What is the air pump for?

check.q: A fighting fish lives in a small bowl with no air pump. How does she get enough oxygen?
options: She gulps air at the surface
She needs less oxygen than other fish
The bowl makes oxygen
check.why: She has a breathing organ above her gills and takes oxygen from gulped air, as a climbing perch does. Choosing 'needs less oxygen' usually means not having noticed her trips to the surface. A bowl must never be filled to a tight lid, because she must reach the air.

flow.context: This is the last step of Gulp Watch. Here you compare the two counts and explain them.

activities.title: Predict the In-between Animal: what should a fossil between fish and frogs look like?
activities.context: Scientists predicted what an animal between fish and four-limbed animals would look like, and how old the rock holding her would be, before they found one. In this activity you make the same prediction with feature cards, and then compare it with the real fossil, Tiktaalik.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
colour pencils

activities.record: Keep your three cards, with the middle card showing your prediction. Beside them write which of your predictions matched Tiktaalik and which did not.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a lobe-finned fish drawn on the left and a four-limbed animal with a flat head drawn on the right, and an empty space with a question mark between them.
setup.caption: 1. Write a card for a lobe-finned fish on the left and one for an early four-limbed animal on the right. Leave a space between.

setup.art: A child drawing an animal in the middle space, with a fish tail and scales, a flat head and two sturdy front fins.
setup.caption: 2. Make a middle card for the animal you would expect in between. Choose each feature.

setup.art: The finished drawing beside a simple outline of Tiktaalik, with ticks next to the features that match.
setup.caption: 3. Compare your prediction with the real fossil.

flow.do: 1. Write a card for the fish with her features: scales, gills, fins with thin rays, no neck, a head shaped like a cone, eyes on the sides. 2. Write a card for an early four-limbed animal with hers: lungs, limbs with fingers, a neck, a flat head, eyes on top. 3. Write '380 million years ago' on the fish card and '365 million years ago' on the other. 4. Put the fish card on the left and the other on the right, with a gap between.
flow.say: Fish like this lived 380 million years ago. Four-limbed animals like this lived 365 million years ago. So what lived in between, and when?
flow.kid: Write each animal's features on a card. Put the cards left and right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Predict the In-between Animal. Here you set out the features of the animals before and after.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to make a middle card for the in-between animal. 2. Ask them to choose the fish form, the later form or a halfway form for each feature. 3. Ask them to write each choice on the card. 4. Ask how old the rock holding such a fossil should be. 5. Ask what kind of place the animal lived in, so we know what kind of rock to search.
flow.say: Make a middle card for the animal you would expect to find. Choose each feature for her. Then think about where she lived.
flow.kid: Make a card for the animal in between. For each feature, choose the fish form, the later form or halfway.

ask.q: What kind of rock would you search, and how old?
good: Rock about 375 million years old, between the two ages.
Rock made from the mud of shallow streams, because she lived at the water's edge.

flow.parent: Any reasoned mixture is a good answer. The point is that a prediction can be made at all, and then tested by digging.
flow.context: This is the main step of Predict the In-between Animal. Here you draw your prediction and say how old the rock should be.

flow.do: 1. Read out what Tiktaalik had: scales, gills and fin rays like a fish. 2. Then read: a flat head, eyes on top, a neck, lungs, and a shoulder, elbow and wrist in each front fin. No fingers. 3. Tell your child the rock was about 375 million years old and formed in shallow streams. 4. Tick each prediction that matched.
flow.say: Here is what the real fossil had. Tick what you predicted correctly. The team chose rock of that age and searched for years before they found her.
flow.kid: Listen to what the real fossil had. Tick what you got right. What surprised you?

check.q: Scientists predicted Tiktaalik's features and the age of her rock before they found her. Why does that matter?
options: A wrong idea would have predicted wrongly
It shows they were lucky
It shows fossils are easy to find
check.why: If four-limbed animals had not evolved from fish, there would be no reason to find such an animal in rock of just that age. A prediction that could have failed, and did not, is strong evidence. Choosing 'lucky' misses that they chose where to dig by reasoning.

flow.context: This is the last step of Predict the In-between Animal. Here you compare your prediction with the real fossil.

projects.title: Five Hundred Million Years on a String: a timeline of the vertebrates
projects.context: You will see how long ago each of these happened, and how late we humans arrive. In this three-day project you stretch a string 5 metres long across a room. Each centimetre stands for one million years. You hang paper flags on it to show when backbones, lungs, limbs, milk and birds first appeared.

materials.item: string or wool, a little over 5 metres
a measuring tape or a ruler
paper for 11 small flags, and colour pencils
clothes pegs or sticky tape

schedule.what: Measure 5 metres of string, fix it along a wall or corridor, and mark the place of each of the 11 events.
Draw and label the 11 flags and peg them at their marks.
Walk the timeline with someone, tell the story, and answer three questions from the string.

projects.record: Take a photograph of the finished timeline, or draw it small in your notebook. Write the three measurements you made on day 3.

setup.art: A child and a parent stretching a long string along a corridor wall, with a measuring tape laid beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fix 5 metres of string along a wall. One end is today. Each centimetre is one million years.

setup.art: A child drawing a small animal on a paper flag, with other finished flags showing a fish, a limbed fish and a small furry animal.
setup.caption: 2. Make a flag for each event.

setup.art: The string with eleven paper flags pegged along it, crowded more closely near the 'today' end, and a child pointing at one.
setup.caption: 3. Peg each flag at its distance from the 'today' end.

flow.do: 1. Cut a string a little longer than 5 metres and fix it along a wall. 2. Mark one end TODAY. 3. Measure from TODAY and make a small mark at each distance below. 4. First vertebrates: 500 centimetres. 5. Bony fish with lungs: 420. 6. Tiktaalik: 375. 7. Acanthostega, with fingers: 365. 8. First animals with an amnion: 320. 9. First mammals: 225. 10. Archaeopteryx, an early bird: 150. 11. Snake and dinosaur eggs in Gujarat: 68. 12. The asteroid that ended the other dinosaurs: 66. 13. Indohyus, a whale relative in Kashmir: 48. 14. First humans of our kind: 3 millimetres.
flow.say: One centimetre is a million years. Before we measure, guess. Where on this string will the first mammals go? Where do we humans start?
flow.kid: Fix the string. One end is today. Measure and mark each event. One centimetre is a million years.
flow.parent: The ages are rounded, and scientists revise them as new fossils are found. If your corridor is short, use 1 centimetre for 2 million years and halve every distance.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Five Hundred Million Years on a String. Here you fix the string and mark where each event belongs.

flow.do: 1. Cut 11 small paper flags. 2. On each, write the name and age of the animal or event. Draw a small picture too, if you like. 3. Peg or tape each flag at its mark. 4. Stand back and look at the spacing.
flow.say: Write the name and age on each flag. When they are all up, stand back. Where are the flags crowded, and where are they far apart?
flow.kid: Write a flag for each event. Peg it at its mark. Where are the flags crowded?
flow.context: This is day 2 of Five Hundred Million Years on a String. Here you make the flags and hang them.

flow.do: 1. Walk from the far end to TODAY and tell the story aloud at each flag. 2. Measure the gap between lungs and fingers. 3. Measure the gap between the first mammals and the asteroid. 4. Measure how much of the string holds humans. 5. Write the three answers.
flow.say: Walk me through it. Then we will measure three gaps. First, how long were there lungs before fingers?
flow.kid: Walk the string and tell the story. Measure three gaps. Write the answers.

ask.q: For how long did mammals live at the same time as the big dinosaurs?
good: About 159 million years, from 225 to 66 million years ago.
Far longer than the time since the asteroid.

check.q: On the string, lungs are at 420 centimetres and fingers at 365. What does this show?
options: Lungs are about 55 million years older than fingers
Fingers are older than lungs
Lungs and fingers appeared together
check.why: 420 − 365 = 55, and each centimetre is a million years. Animals had lungs for about 55 million years before any had fingers. Choosing 'together' usually means thinking of land animals, who have both.

flow.context: This is day 3 of Five Hundred Million Years on a String. Here you tell the story of the timeline and measure three gaps.

challenges.title: A Fin That Can Do a Push-up
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A carp's fin is a fan of thin rays, good for steering in water. Tiktaalik's front fin had a few sturdy bones with joints, and she could prop herself up on it. Here you build both kinds and test which can hold up a body.
challenges.problem: Build a front fin that can hold a 'body' weighing about 200 grams at least 5 centimetres above the table. The fin must bend in two places, like an elbow and a wrist, so that the body can be lowered to the table and pushed up again.
constraints: The body is a 200 gram packet, such as a small packet of salt, dal or tea.
The fin holds the body at least 5 centimetres above the table for 10 seconds.
The fin bends in two places and does not come apart when you lower and raise the body.
You may use only cardboard, broom sticks or toothpicks, rubber bands and tape.
materials: thin sticks from a coconut-leaf broom, or toothpicks
a 200 gram packet of salt, dal or tea
general: Cut three strips of cardboard for an upper bone, a lower part and a hand, and join them with tape hinges.
Fold each cardboard strip lengthwise into a V, so that it does not buckle.
Use two strips side by side for the lower part, like the two bones in your forearm.
creative: Stretch a rubber band across each joint as a muscle, so that the fin springs back up after you press the body down.
Make the hand from several short pieces fanned out, like the many small bones in a wrist, so that it sits flat on the table.
Build a pair of fins joined by a cardboard shoulder, so that the body rests between them as Tiktaalik's chest did.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Plan the fin first: draw it and label the joints, or lay out the strips and point to the joints. Build it, rest the packet on top and measure the height. Lower the body to the table and push it up five times. Where does your fin fail first, and how would you make that place stronger?
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the thick cardboard. Broom sticks have sharp ends, so keep them away from faces.

setup.art: A fan of twelve thin broom sticks taped together at one end, standing on the table with a small packet of salt being lowered onto it and the sticks splaying outward.
setup.caption: 1. First build a fan fin of thin sticks. Try to rest the packet on it.

setup.art: Three folded cardboard strips joined end to end with tape hinges, labelled upper bone, lower bones and hand.
setup.caption: 2. Then build a fin with a few sturdy parts and two joints.

setup.art: The jointed cardboard fin propped on the table with the packet resting on top and a ruler showing 6 centimetres.
setup.caption: 3. Rest the packet on top and measure the height.

flow.do: 1. Tape twelve thin sticks together at one end to make a fan, like a carp's fin. 2. Stand the fan on its tips and rest the packet on the taped end. 3. Watch what the sticks do. 4. Ask what this fin is good for, and what it lacks.
flow.say: This is a fan fin, like a carp's. Rest the body on it. What happens? What is a fin like this good at?
flow.kid: Tape twelve sticks into a fan. Rest the packet on it. What happens to the sticks?
flow.parent: The thin rays splay or snap. A fan fin is light and makes a wide paddle for steering in water, where the water holds the body up.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Fin That Can Do a Push-up. Here you build a fan fin of thin rays and find out that it holds no weight.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to feel the bones of their own arm: one, then two, then many small ones. 2. Ask them to say where the two joints of a fin on that pattern should go. 3. A grown-up cuts the cardboard strips. 4. Your child folds, joins and tapes the fin. 5. Test it with the packet as you build.
flow.say: Feel your arm. One bone, then two, then many small ones. Think of a fin on that pattern. Where will it bend? Then build it.
flow.kid: Feel the bones in your arm. Plan a fin with two joints. Build it from cardboard and tape.
flow.context: This is the building step of A Fin That Can Do a Push-up. Here you design and build a fin with a few sturdy parts and two joints.

flow.do: 1. Rest the packet on the fin and measure its height above the table. 2. Time 10 seconds. 3. Lower the body to the table and push it up again, five times. 4. Note where the fin bends or fails.
flow.say: Does it hold for ten seconds? How high? Now do five push-ups with it. Where does it give way first?
flow.kid: Rest the packet on your fin. Measure the height. Do five push-ups. Where does it fail?
flow.context: This is the testing step of A Fin That Can Do a Push-up. Here you test whether your fin holds the body up and bends without breaking.

flow.do: 1. Compare the fan fin and the jointed fin. 2. Ask what each is good for. 3. Ask why an animal in shallow water might do better with the jointed kind.
flow.say: Neither fin is the better one everywhere. Where does the fan win? Where does the jointed fin win? What would Tiktaalik use hers for?
flow.kid: Which fin is better for steering in deep water? Which is better for propping up in the shallows?

check.q: Why could Tiktaalik prop herself up on her front fins when a carp cannot?
options: Her fins had sturdy bones with joints
Her fins were longer
She weighed less than a carp
check.why: Each front fin had a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist made of sturdy bones, so it could bear weight and bend. A carp's fin is a fan of thin rays. Choosing 'longer' usually means thinking about size and missing what is inside the fin.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Fin That Can Do a Push-up. Here you compare the two fins and say what each is good for.

worksheets.title: In-between animals: air-breathing fish and egg-laying mammals (core)

items.p: Why do the five groups of vertebrates share so many features?
opts: They live in the same places
items.why: All vertebrates descend from one group of fish-like animals who lived about 500 million years ago. Shared features such as the backbone were inherited from them.

items.p: True or false: every mammal is born alive.
items.why: False. The platypus and the four echidnas are mammals, and they lay eggs. They have fur and feed their young on milk.

items.p: A mammal who lays eggs is called a ____.
items.why: The five monotremes are the platypus and four kinds of echidna.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Ancestor
a relative from long ago from whom you descend
Tetrapod
a vertebrate with four limbs, or with four-limbed ancestors
Fossil
what is left of a living being from long ago, kept in rock
Amnion
the bag of water a baby reptile, bird or mammal grows in
Vestigial part
a small leftover of a part that did more in ancestors
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: Sort these fish: breathes with gills only, or also breathes air.
items.why: The murrel and the climbing perch gulp air into a chamber above the gills. The lungfish has lungs. The mudskipper takes in oxygen through her wet skin and mouth lining.

items.p: Put these features in the order in which they first appeared.
items.why: This is the order of the steps in the Feature Ladder. No animal has a later feature without the earlier ones.

items.p: Bubbles appeared in cold water as it warmed up. What does this show?
opts: Warm water holds less dissolved air
Cold water has no air in it
items.why: The cold water held more dissolved air than it could keep once it warmed, so the extra came out as bubbles. Choosing 'makes new air' misses that nothing was added to the water.

items.p: A murrel lives for a week in damp mud. Carp die in a warm, shrinking pool. Explain why.
items.a: The murrel gulps air into a chamber above her gills, so she needs dampness and air, not deep water. The carp have gills only. Warm, shallow water holds very little dissolved oxygen, so they cannot get enough.
items.why: A strong answer says how each fish gets oxygen, and says that warm water holds little of it.

items.p: Acanthostega had 8 fingers on each hand. How many fingers did she have on two hands?
items.why: 8 + 8 = 16. Five fingers on a hand came later.

items.p: Draw the bones inside your arm, from shoulder to fingertips. Show one bone, two bones, many small bones, then fingers.
items.art: An empty outline of a child's arm and hand, palm up.
items.a: One long bone in the upper arm, two side by side in the forearm, a cluster of small bones at the wrist, then the bones of five fingers.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the pattern in order. The same pattern is in a frog's leg, a crow's wing and a whale's flipper, because all inherited it from one ancestor.

items.p: Three of these are mammals. Which one is not?
items.why: A penguin is a bird, with feathers and no milk. The platypus and the echidna lay eggs, but they have fur and milk, so they are mammals.

items.p: True or false: a crocodile is a closer relative of a crow than of a lizard.
items.why: True. Crocodiles and birds share an ancestor who is not an ancestor of lizards. Crocodiles look like lizards because both kept old features, such as scales.

items.p: Which feature has arisen many separate times among vertebrates?
items.why: Live birth arose more than 150 separate times, mostly in lizards and snakes. Milk, feathers and the backbone each arose once.

items.p: Draw a platypus. Label three features that make her a mammal, and one that most mammals lack.
items.art: A blank space for the child's own drawing of a platypus, with four empty label lines.
a: A body that makes its own heat
items.why: A strong answer names fur and milk. Egg-laying is the feature most mammals lack. The bill and webbed feet are her own special features. Her group is decided by fur and milk.

items.p: Three people talk about the platypus.

views.says: Mammals are born alive. She lays eggs, so she is not a real mammal.
She is a mammal. The rule 'mammals are born alive' was too simple.
Rules come second. She is on the mammal branch of the family tree, so she is a mammal.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use your Feature Ladder as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the Feature Ladder: the platypus has fur and milk, and her row differs from the cow's by one feature only. It chooses a view, gives that evidence, and says what another view has right.
items.why: The child is right that she breaks a common rule. The teacher is right that the rule was made from too few animals. The biologist explains why: groups are branches, and rules are our short descriptions of them.

items.p: What did the fossil Acanthostega show about the first limbs with fingers?
opts: They were for running on land
items.why: She had limbs with eight fingers, and also gills, weak ribs and elbows that could not bend forward. She lived in water. Choosing 'running on land' is the old idea her fossil overturned.

items.p: Explain how the platypus shows that milk is older than birth without an egg.
items.a: The platypus makes milk and still lays eggs. Her branch split from ours after milk evolved. If birth without an egg had come first, an egg-laying mammal with milk would be hard to explain. All mammals share the same milk genes, so milk was there in their shared ancestor.
items.why: A strong answer uses the order of branching: a feature shared by both branches was present before the split.

items.p: Why is 'born alive' a poor clue to which animals are close relatives?
items.why: Vipers, some sharks, guppies and cows all bear live young, but they are not close relatives. The feature arose separately in each branch.

items.p: When the same feature arises separately in animals who are not close relatives, it is called ____ evolution.
items.why: Convergent means 'coming together'. Wings in bats and birds are an example.

items.p: True or false: the platypus stopped evolving long ago.
items.why: False. Her branch has evolved for as long as ours, and gained new features such as a bill that senses electric signals. She kept one old feature, egg-laying.

items.p: Sort each likeness: inherited from a shared ancestor, or arose separately.
items: arm bones of a human and a bat
wings of a bat and a crow
milk of a cow and a platypus
live birth in a viper and a cow
smooth shape of a dolphin and a shark
feathers of a crow and a penguin
items.why: A likeness from a shared ancestor is a clue to the family tree. A likeness that arose separately is a clue to a shared way of living.

items.p: A litre of air holds 270 milligrams of oxygen. A litre of water holds 9. How many times more is that?
items.why: 270 ÷ 9 = 30. Air holds about 30 times as much oxygen as the same amount of water, which is why gulping air helps a fish so much.

items.p: Match each animal to the surprise she holds.
pairs: Murrel
a fish who can drown
Echidna
a mammal who carries her egg in a pouch
Russell's viper
a snake who bears live young
Indohyus
a four-legged relative of the first whales
Tiktaalik
a fish with a neck and wrists
items.why: Each of these animals has a feature we do not expect from her group. Each one makes sense once the groups are seen as branches of one tree.

items.p: A friend says a cow is 'more evolved' than a carp. What would you tell them?
items.a: Both have been evolving for exactly the same length of time since their shared ancestor. The cow's branch gained limbs, an amnion and milk. The carp's branch gained its own features, such as the swim bladder and fan fins. The family tree has branches, not a top.
items.why: A strong answer says that every living animal is equally modern, and names a feature that the carp's branch gained.

items.p: Which of these is evidence that your ancestors had thick fur?
items.why: A tiny muscle raises each hair when you are cold. On a furry animal this fluffs the coat. On us it does almost nothing, so it is a leftover.

items.p: Draw a small family tree for a lizard, a crocodile and a crow. Show which two are closest.
items.art: Three small pictures at the top of a blank space: a lizard, a crocodile and a crow.
items.a: The crocodile and the crow join at one fork. That fork then joins the lizard's line further down.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the crocodile with the crow. Putting the crocodile with the lizard goes by scales and shape, which are old features.

items.p: Put these animals in order, from your most distant relative to your closest.
items.why: Each one shares one more step of the family tree with you than the one before. The platypus is a mammal, so she is the closest of these.

items.p: Three of these have four limbs, or had ancestors with four limbs. Which one does not?
items.why: A seahorse is a fish with thin fan fins, and her ancestors never had four limbs. Snakes, whales and caecilians lost limbs that their ancestors had.

items.p: Scientists compare the DNA of two animals and find few differences. What does that suggest?
opts: They live in the same place
items.why: Copying mistakes build up over time. Few differences means little time on separate branches.

items.p: Two scientists talk about the word 'reptile'.

views.says: A group should be a whole branch. Birds grew from the reptile branch, so birds are reptiles.
'Reptile' is a useful word for scaly animals who bask. Keep it, and remember it is not a whole branch.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more, and why? Then give one good point of the other view.
items.a: A strong answer chooses one view and gives a reason from the family tree or from everyday use. It also says what the other view gets right.
items.why: Both scientists accept the same family tree. They disagree about what names are for: showing who is related, or describing a way of living.

worksheets.title: In-between animals: argued ideas and deep time (challenge)

items.p: Lungs and limbs came before life on land. Give two ideas for why limbed animals first left the water.
items.a: One idea: the banks had food, such as insects and millipedes, and no big hunters. Another: warm shallows held little oxygen, and a raised head could reach the air. An older idea, that they crawled between drying ponds, is now doubted.
items.why: A strong answer gives two ideas and treats them as ideas. Nobody knows for certain.

items.p: Humans carry broken genes for making egg yolk. What is the best explanation?
opts: Our distant ancestors laid yolky eggs
Humans will lay eggs one day
We get them from eating eggs
items.why: The early ancestors of mammals laid eggs with yolk. After milk took over the feeding of young, the yolk genes were no longer needed and stopped working. Genes do not come from food.

items.p: One centimetre is 1 million years. Tiktaalik is at 375 and Acanthostega at 365. How many centimetres apart?
items.why: 375 − 365 = 10 centimetres, which stands for 10 million years.

items.p: Bones and DNA were studied separately, and they give the same family tree. Why is that strong evidence?
items.a: The two kinds of evidence do not depend on each other. If the tree were wrong, there would be no reason for them to agree. Since they agree in almost every place, the tree is very likely real.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two methods are separate, so their agreement is not a coincidence.

items.p: True or false: lungs evolved from the swim bladders of fish.
items.why: False, as far as the evidence shows. Lungfish and bichirs, on two early branches, both have lungs. So the first bony fish probably had lungs, and the swim bladder is a changed lung.

items.p: The purple frog's closest relatives live on the Seychelles islands. What explains this best?
opts: The land they lived on split apart
items.why: India and the Seychelles were once joined. The land split and drifted apart with the frogs' ancestors on both pieces. Frogs cannot survive in sea water for long.

items.p: Sort these: scientists agree, or scientists still argue.
items: Four-limbed animals came from lobe-finned fish
Why limbed animals first left the water
What the first milk was for
Warm water holds less oxygen than cold
items.why: Scientists agree on the family tree itself. They still argue about the reasons for some changes, and about how to name the groups.

items.p: Draw an animal halfway between a fish and a frog. Label three fish features and three newer features.
items.art: A blank space with a small fish drawn at the left edge and a small frog at the right edge.
items.a: Fish features could be scales, gills and fin rays. Newer features could be a neck, a flat head with eyes on top, and sturdy front fins with a wrist.
items.why: A strong drawing mixes old and new features in one body, as Tiktaalik did. Any reasoned mixture is acceptable.

items.p: A small leftover of a part that was bigger in an animal's ancestors is called a ____ part.
items.why: The human tailbone and the small hip bones of a whale are vestigial parts.

items.p: Put these in order, from the oldest to the most recent.
items.why: About 500, 375, 225, 150 and 66 million years ago. Mammals are older than birds, which surprises many people.

items.p: If every in-between animal were still alive, could we sort vertebrates into five groups? Explain.
items.a: It would be very hard. Each animal would be only a little different from her nearest relatives, so there would be no gaps to draw lines in. The groups look separate today because most of the in-between animals died out.
items.why: A strong answer says that the gaps between groups come from extinction. Any answer that reasons from this is good, whichever way it concludes.

items.p: Water holds 11.3 milligrams of oxygen per litre at 10 °C and 7.6 at 30 °C. What fraction is lost?
items.why: 11.3 − 7.6 = 3.7. And 3.7 out of 11.3 is close to one third. So a pond at 30 °C holds about a third less oxygen than one at 10 °C.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it suggests.
pairs: A fossil with both gills and fingers
the first limbs were used in water
Lungs in both lungfish and bichirs
the first bony fish had lungs
Broken yolk genes in humans
our ancestors laid eggs with yolk
Small hip bones inside a whale
her ancestors had back legs
Nest-guarding in crocodiles and birds
their shared ancestor may have guarded nests
items.why: Each line goes from something that can be seen to a conclusion about the past. A strong answer could say how sure each conclusion is.

items.p: Draw a murrel's head from the side. Label the gills, the air chamber, and her mouth at the surface.
items.art: A blank space for the child's own drawing, with a wavy line near the top for the water surface.

items.p: Three ideas about why limbed animals first left the water.

views.says: Ponds dried up. The ones who could crawl to the next pond lived.
The banks had food and no big hunters. Going there paid off.
Warm shallows had little oxygen. A raised head could reach the air.

items.ask: Which idea do you find strongest? Give one piece of evidence for it, and one problem with another idea.
items.a: A strong answer picks one idea and uses evidence from the unit: the first limbs were too weak for crawling, the fossils come from wet wooded places, insects were on land already, and warm water holds little oxygen.
items.why: Most scientists now doubt the drying ponds idea. The other two are both taken seriously, and both may be partly right.

quiz.p: A murrel is kept in a pot filled to the brim, under a tight lid. What is the danger?
opts: She cannot reach air and may drown
She has no room to turn
quiz.why: A murrel must gulp air at the surface. With no air gap she cannot breathe properly, even though she is in water.

quiz.p: Which holds more oxygen: a litre of air or a litre of pond water?
quiz.why: Air is about one-fifth oxygen. Water holds only a little dissolved oxygen, about 9 milligrams in a litre at 20 °C.

quiz.p: Which came first in the history of animals?
quiz.why: Lungfish have lungs and no legs, and every animal with four limbs has lungs. Fossils agree: fish had lungs long before any had limbs.

quiz.p: Which animal shows that milk evolved before mammals stopped laying eggs?
quiz.why: The platypus lays eggs and feeds her hatched young on milk. A kangaroo is born alive, and a penguin is a bird with no milk.

quiz.p: Tiktaalik had gills and scales, and also a neck and wrists. What is such a fossil called?
quiz.why: A transitional fossil has features of an older group and of a newer group. It shows what the animals in between were like.

quiz.p: Which of these is the closest living relative of a crow?
quiz.why: Crocodiles and birds share an ancestor that lizards and snakes do not. A bat flies, but she is a mammal.

quiz.p: Bats and birds both have wings. Why is this not a sign that they are close relatives?
opts: Bats are a kind of bird
Wings are a very old feature
quiz.why: Their shared ancestor had no wings. Each branch evolved wings separately, which is called convergent evolution.

quiz.p: True or false: the steps of the Feature Ladder show which animals are better.
quiz.why: False. The steps show the order in which features first appeared. Every animal on the ladder is alive today and has evolved for the same length of time.

quiz.p: Which part of your body is the leftover of a tail?
quiz.why: The tailbone is three to five small joined bones at the end of the backbone. The navel is where the cord from the placenta joined you.

quiz.p: Why do fish in a warm, shallow pond gasp at the surface at dawn?
opts: The water has very little dissolved oxygen
quiz.why: Warm water holds little oxygen, and plants and rotting leaves use it up overnight. The thin top layer of water, next to the air, has the most.

quiz.p: A fossil has feathers, and also teeth and a long bony tail. What does it most likely show?
opts: An animal between older dinosaurs and birds
A bird that grew teeth by mistake
quiz.why: Feathers are a bird feature. Teeth and a long bony tail are older dinosaur features. Archaeopteryx, about 150 million years old, is such an animal.

quiz.p: In the Air in Water test, what had to stay the same for all three tumblers?
opts: The tumbler, the amount and the place
Only the colour of the tumbler
How cold the water was at the start
quiz.why: Only the water's history was changed: cold, room-warm or boiled. Everything else was kept the same, so any difference in bubbles came from that one change.

applications: Fish farmers pump air into ponds on hot nights, because warm water holds little oxygen. Farmers of murrel and climbing perch can keep them in shallow, still ponds, because these fish breathe air.
Live murrels and climbing perches are carried to market in wet baskets with very little water, so they reach the buyer fresh.
Anyone who keeps a fighting fish or a gourami must leave an air gap under the lid, because these fish gulp air.
Doctors and scientists learn about human bodies from mice, zebrafish and frogs. This works because we share ancestors with them, and so we share most of our genes and organs.
Fossil hunters, like those who found Tiktaalik, choose where to dig by working out how old the rock must be and what kind of place it formed in.
Wildlife officers use DNA to find out which animal a piece of meat, skin or fish came from.
People who protect nature give special care to animals on old, lonely branches of the family tree, such as the purple frog and the caecilians of India.

open_questions.q: Why did animals with limbs first come out of the water?
open_questions.why_open: Limbs and lungs were there already. Fossils show bodies and the places they lived, but they do not show reasons. Food on the banks, safety from hunters and easier breathing are all possible.

open_questions.q: What was the very first milk for?
open_questions.why_open: Milk does not fossilise. One idea is that it kept soft-shelled eggs moist and free of germs. Another is that it fed the hatched young from the start. The genes give hints and no clear answer.

open_questions.q: How many separate times did fish evolve a way to breathe air?
open_questions.why_open: Air breathing is found in many branches of fish, with different organs in each. Scientists count dozens of separate origins, and the count changes as more fish are studied.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a platypus to sense the electric signals of a prawn?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure the sensors in her bill and how her brain uses them. Nobody can know from outside what the sense feels like to her.

open_questions.q: Why did one branch of mammals keep laying eggs for 160 million years or more?
open_questions.why_open: Egg-laying clearly works well for the platypus and the echidnas. Whether something about their way of living favoured it, or whether live birth simply never arose in their branch, is not known.

open_questions.q: Is a group of animals something real in nature, or a line that people draw?
open_questions.why_open: Branches of the family tree are real. But where one group ends and the next begins depends on which in-between animals have died out, and on what we choose to name.

maths.problem: A litre of air holds about 270 milligrams of oxygen. A litre of pond water at 20 °C holds about 9 milligrams. How many litres of water must pass over a fish's gills to bring as much oxygen as one litre of air?
maths.explain: 270 ÷ 9 = 30. One litre of air holds as much oxygen as 30 litres of water. So one gulp of air is worth many mouthfuls of water.
maths.context: This is about the Air in Water test, where you saw that water holds dissolved air, and that warm water holds less of it.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one amount by the other shows how big the advantage of breathing air is, which bubbles alone cannot show.

maths.problem: A litre of fresh water holds about 11.3 milligrams of oxygen at 10 °C, 9.1 at 20 °C and 7.6 at 30 °C. Does the amount fall by the same number for each 10 degrees? Predict the amount at 40 °C.
maths.answer: No. The fall gets smaller each time. A good prediction for 40 °C is between 6 and 7 milligrams. The measured value is about 6.4.
maths.explain: From 10 to 20 °C the fall is 11.3 − 9.1 = 2.2. From 20 to 30 °C it is 9.1 − 7.6 = 1.5. The second fall is smaller. If the next fall is smaller again, about 1.0 to 1.2, the amount at 40 °C is about 6.4 to 6.6.
maths.context: This is about the Air in Water test, where cold water gave up bubbles of air as it warmed.
maths.why_maths: Looking at how the differences change lets you predict a temperature you never measured, and a curve on a graph shows the same thing at a glance.

maths.problem: In your Feature Ladder table, 6 animals have lungs and 5 have four limbs. Is every animal with four limbs also in the group with lungs? Is every animal with lungs also in the group with four limbs? What does this tell you?
maths.answer: Every animal with four limbs has lungs. Not every animal with lungs has four limbs, because the lungfish has lungs and no limbs. So lungs came first.
maths.explain: Draw a big circle for the 6 animals with lungs. The 5 animals with four limbs all fit inside it, in a smaller circle. One animal, the lungfish, is in the big circle and outside the small one. A feature that arrived later is always found inside the group that has the earlier feature.
maths.context: This is about the Feature Ladder, where you ticked the features of seven animals in a table.
maths.why_maths: Circles inside circles show at once which feature is older, without any dates.

maths.problem: On the string timeline, the first mammals are at 225 centimetres and the asteroid strike at 66. For what fraction of their history, to the nearest tenth, did mammals live beside the big dinosaurs?
maths.explain: Mammals and big dinosaurs shared the Earth for 225 − 66 = 159 million years. The whole history of mammals is 225 million years. 159 ÷ 225 is about 0.7, or seven tenths. Mammals have lived without the big dinosaurs for only the last three tenths.
maths.context: This is about Five Hundred Million Years on a String, the timeline where one centimetre stands for one million years.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of mammal history was spent beside dinosaurs, which two separate dates do not show.

maths.problem: In a made-up Lap or Suck test, a child lapping from a plate drank 1 tablespoon in 20 seconds. Through a straw she drank 4 tablespoons in 8 seconds. How many times faster was the straw?
maths.explain: Lapping: 1 tablespoon in 20 seconds. Straw: 4 tablespoons in 8 seconds, which is 1 tablespoon in 2 seconds. 20 ÷ 2 = 10. The straw delivered water 10 times as fast.
maths.context: This is about Lap or Suck, where you drank water from a plate, from a wet cloth and through a straw.
maths.why_maths: The two tries lasted different times, so the amounts cannot be compared directly. Working out the time for one tablespoon makes the comparison fair.

maths.problem: Giving birth to live young arose about 150 separate times among vertebrates. About 115 of these were in lizards and snakes, and 1 was in mammals. Roughly what fraction arose in lizards and snakes?
maths.explain: 115 out of 150 is 23 out of 30, which is a little more than 0.75. So about three quarters of all the separate beginnings of live birth were in lizards and snakes.
maths.context: This is about the card 'The same feature can arise many times', which says that live birth is a poor clue to family.
maths.why_maths: The fraction shows that live birth is mainly a lizard and snake story, although we think of it as a mammal feature.

maths.problem: In Count the Differences, the cow string differs from the human string in 2 places and the hen string in 4. None of the places are the same. Predict how many places differ between the cow and the hen. Then count.
maths.explain: The cow has 2 changes that the human lacks, and the hen has 4 different ones. Going from the hen to the cow, you pass all 4 and then all 2. 4 + 2 = 6. Counting the two strings square by square also gives 6.
maths.context: This is about Count the Differences, where you compared five made-up letter strings that stand for DNA.
maths.why_maths: If the family tree is right, the counts must add up along its branches. Predicting a count and then checking it tests the tree.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what the first legs were for? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time scientists thought they knew why fish grew legs. In the last century the American scientist Alfred Romer pictured fish stranded in drying ponds. Those with stronger fins could crawl to the next pond, and over many generations their fins became legs. So legs were for walking on land. In 1987 Jenny Clack, a British scientist, led a small team to East Greenland. They brought back blocks of rock holding an animal called Acanthostega, about 365 million years old. In Cambridge the bones were slowly freed from the rock, which took years. In 1990 Clack and Michael Coates reported that the hand had eight fingers. In 1991 they reported that she had gills like a fish. Her elbows could not bend forward, and her ribs were too short to hold up her chest out of water. Here was an animal with legs and fingers who lived in water. So legs came first, and walking on land came later.
how_we_found_out.who: Jenny Clack and Michael Coates, with the team who collected the fossils in East Greenland. Alfred Romer was the best-known supporter of the earlier idea.
how_we_found_out.when: 1987 (the fossils collected), 1990 (eight fingers reported) and 1991 (gills reported)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That legs evolved for walking on land, in fish who had to crawl from one drying pond to the next. Acanthostega had legs with fingers, and also gills and a body too weak for land, so the first legs were used in water.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in a warm jacket kneeling on a rocky slope in Greenland, brushing dust from a block of red-brown rock in which the outline of a small limb with many fingers can be seen.

roots.context: We have been learning about animals who seem to sit between two groups, and about the order in which features arrived. Now we ask what that order tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Feature Ladder, the lungfish had lungs and no legs. The platypus had milk and still laid eggs. So lungs are older than legs, and milk is older than birth without an egg. The features of each group arrived one at a time, over millions of years. An in-between animal is no mistake, because she shows us that order.
deep_truth.habit: We learn each group as a fixed list that comes as one set: a mammal has fur, gives milk and is born alive. Then an animal with only part of the list looks like a rule-breaker. But the list was never one set. Each feature on it began at a different time, in a different ancestor.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Feature Ladder, no animal had a later feature without all the earlier ones, and the ticks made a staircase. The lungfish and the platypus each stood one step short of a group. The platypus's DNA has milk genes shared with every mammal and one working yolk gene. Human DNA still holds the broken remains of yolk genes.

three.who_am_i: Your body is made of features of very different ages. Your backbone is about 500 million years old. Your lungs are more than 400 million, your fingers about 365 million, and your milk-drinking more than 200 million.
three.what_is_life: Life does not make new kinds of animals from nothing. It changes what is already there. A lung became a swim bladder, a fin became an arm, and a tail became a tailbone.
three.what_is_this_world: Every animal with a backbone is your relative. The names of the five groups mark the places where one family branched.

roots.thread: All vertebrates descend from one population of small, fish-like animals who lived about 500 million years ago. That one family became the many: sardines, frogs, crocodiles, crows, platypuses and us. The groups look separate only because most of the relatives in between have died out. When one of them turns up, alive like the platypus or in rock like Tiktaalik, we can see the join. Everything is conscious, so each branch is also one more way of being aware of the same world.

teachings.link: People sorted animals into groups long before they knew about evolution. Darwin saw why the sorting worked: the groups were families all along.

teachings.teaching: The name that can be spoken is not the lasting name. Naming is the mother of the ten thousand things.
teachings.link: We named five groups, and then the platypus did not fit. The animals were never divided as sharply as our names for them.
