science.text: All vertebrates share a common ancestor. Fossils and DNA, studied separately, give the same family tree.
The features that define each group arose at different times. Lungs came before limbs, and milk before birth without an egg.
Whether groups such as 'reptiles' or 'fish' are real things in nature, or useful lines that people draw, is still argued by biologists and philosophers.

other_view.who: Georges Cuvier, the French scientist who founded the study of fossil animals
other_view.view: Cuvier held that every part of an animal fits every other part so closely that one part cannot change alone. A meat-eater's teeth need a meat-eater's claws and gut. So he thought a body could not be rebuilt piece by piece, and that each kind of animal had stayed the same from the beginning. He knew more about animal bodies than anyone of his time, and he was right that the parts must work together. The in-between fossils that answer him were found long after he died in 1832.

practice.title: Four old parts
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Put a hand on your back and feel your backbone. It is about 500 million years old. Now breathe in slowly and feel your lungs fill. They are more than 400 million years old. Spread your fingers wide. They are about 365 million years old. Now feel the hair on your arm, which is a mammal's fur. Take three slow breaths. All of these came to you from animals you will never meet. Open your eyes.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Feel your backbone with one hand. Breathe in and feel your lungs. Spread your fingers wide. Touch the hair on your arm. Each part is millions of years old. Take three slow breaths. Open your eyes.

ask: Your mother's mother's mother, far enough back, was a fish. At which mother do you think 'fish' stopped?
The platypus did not fit the rule for mammals. Was the platypus wrong, or the rule?
If every in-between animal were still alive, would there be five groups, or one long family?
Your backbone is 500 million years old, and you were born about ten years ago. How old are you, really?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this lesson were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried in a kitchen, so please treat the amounts and times as a starting point. Air in Water is on the main path. It needs three matching clear glasses, a fridge and a stove, and the three waters must be made ready at least 3 hours before the test, so start in the morning. The result depends on how much warmer the window is than the fridge. In a warm Indian room, fridge-cold shaken water should cover the glass with small bubbles within 40 to 60 minutes, and boiled water should show none. If the cold glass shows very few, wait another hour or use an older, scratched glass. On a very cool day the effect is weaker. The bubbles are air, and the test does not measure oxygen itself. The Feature Ladder needs only paper, and its rows must come to 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5 and 6 ticks. Lap or Suck is wet and a little silly, so put a towel down. The cloth never gives back all its water when squeezed, and the step says so. It is a model of one idea about teats, and not proof of it. Old Parts in Your Body may find nobody at home without the wrist tendon, which is a normal result for a small group. Count the Differences uses made-up letter strings, and the counts must be 2, 4, 5 and 7. Gulp Watch needs an aquarium or a pet shop, so it is an extra. The fin challenge needs a grown-up to cut cardboard. Closest Cousins uses simplified addresses: the three mammals with a full placenta come out equally close, although bats and dolphins are in fact a little closer to each other than to us. Nothing on the main path needs a garden. Facts checked against sources while writing: the ages and finders of Tiktaalik, Acanthostega, Indohyus and the snake Sanajeh, the platypus's eggs, milk, body temperature and sensors, the yolk gene study of 2008, the counts of live birth, the oxygen figures for water, Margaret Dayhoff's work, the Chikilidae caecilians, the coelacanth of 1938, and Romer's drying ponds idea. Facts a person may wish to check again: that a murrel held under water with no air can drown (one biodiversity database says so, and no test was found), the figure of about 270 milligrams of oxygen in a litre of air (worked out here from the make-up of air), the monotreme split of 160 to 220 million years (sources differ), and the ages on the string timeline, which are rounded. The quotations from Darwin and the Tao Te Ching are paraphrases. The three films were confirmed by address, title and channel, and were not watched from here.
